In the Brahmayāmala, regarding the festival of the Mothers:
Hari says, "Oṃ!
I shall describe the festival of the Mothers; listen, O Brahmā, according to the proper sequence."
Formerly, at the beginning of the Kṛtayuga, the gods were [confronted] by the lords of Śira and Maima.
O great king, having been obstructed by the gods and by Dāruka,
all the gods reflected upon the cause of that which was called Dāruka.
"O venerable one, how did Dāruka bring Hari?
Having heard that, Hari was addressed; tell us how he created a woman."
Having heard this from the God, Brahmā indeed created each woman according to her nature:
the Brahmanī was born from Brahmā, and the Māheśvarī from Maheśvara.
Kaumārī is born from Skanda; Vaiṣṇavī is born from Viṣṇu;
Vārāhī is born from Yama; and Indrāṇī is born from Indra.
O God, these mothers indeed fought with Dāruka;
yet the mighty great Asura overcame the weak mothers by means of his superior strength.
Arising from the collective union of the Mothers, she is the supreme beyond the single hero;
thus, O Eye of the Supreme Lord, she is indeed a portion of the Supreme.
Then Bhadrakālī was born, the slayer of Dāruka;
having pierced Dāruka’s heart, she [drank] blood smeared with flesh.
Having begun with the words "O you who take away all that fills the heart," the Lord,
having heard that, performed a dance and became pacified.
May there be peace from all the gods, O Supreme Goddess Cāmuṇḍā!
Listen now to the distinction of their forms in each Brahma-age.
In the Kṛta Yuga, ten million forms are proclaimed;
[the principal ones are] Prakarālyā, Titīkṣṇākṣī, Vidyujjihvā, and Vijṛmbhiṇī.
She is indeed the agitating one and the deluding one, and likewise she is the one whose face is the womb;
she is renowned as the downward-facing one, and likewise she is the fierce-faced one.
Kṛṣṇā, Kṛṣṇākṣī, and likewise Śyāmalā;
Tryambakī, Gomukhī, and another known as Sneha.
The sixteen forms renowned as being oriented toward the Bhaga are remembered;
these forms are to be known as the Mātṛkās and are thus proclaimed.
The black should be known as even blacker; the white becomes whiter than white.
The red should be known as even redder; the yellow becomes yellower than yellow.
The forms are to be known as renowned; they are proclaimed to be the embodiments [of the Goddess].
Bhadrakālī is indeed Cāmuṇḍī, who always increases victory.
The one arising from the head is proclaimed as Nāśai in the Kali Yuga;
by these [names] the forms are to be known, and it shall always bring peace.
One should worship her with every effort in her fourfold form;
she brings about peace for ten years, and victory shall come to kings.
One should perform the worship of the Mothers according to the ritual procedure for the fourfold prosperity— a rite that removes all sins, is peaceful, and always brings about victory.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Festival of the Mothers," in the *Brahmayāmala*, the compendium of one hundred thousand verses.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the supreme procedure for the command of the Goddess.
In the village and in the city, as well as in the town and even in the market-town.
At a sacred ford, or in a pleasant place, by the ocean, on the flanks of mountains,
on a mountain, in a forest, or at the confluence of rivers.
In the east, there is victory for Indra; in the southeast, there shall be fear of fire;
in the south, premature death; and in the southwest, affliction by disease.
In the west (Vāruṇī), there is the destruction of rain; in the northwest (Vāyavyā), disease shall enter;
in the north (Saumyā), there is complete success; and in the northeast (Aiśānī), it bestows the eight siddhis.
Outside the northern gate, to the east of the Soma-sūtra,
having established an interval of one hundred daṇḍas, there is the supreme place that grants all siddhis.
At the eastern gate there is victory, but at the southeast there will be death;
at the gate of Yama (the south) there is strife, while at the southwest one enters destruction.
In the west, there shall be the attainment of all siddhis; in the northwest, the destruction of enemies. Among these, the northern door represents progressively higher sovereignty.
This door is prescribed at the entrance of Īśa for the purpose of protection;
it is fourfold, consisting of the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra.
For the sake of destroying the sins of Brahmins, a Kṣatriya shall attain victory;
a Vaiśya obtains wealth, and a Śūdra shall obtain happiness.
One should perform the ritual acquisition (parigraha) over as wide an area as the extent of the palace;
one should have the ground ploughed there and indicate the sprouts of the seeds.
One should dig a pit one man’s height deep, or even reaching to the navel;
one should fill it with earth, or else fill it with water beforehand.
The preceptor, together with artisans, should determine the solid ground marked by the elephant’s footprint;
in the month of Caitra, he should establish the equinox and indicate the eastward direction for the commencement of the construction.
Having grasped the northern direction there, one should mark out a square;
thus the ground is consecrated, bringing about the great eight siddhis.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Seizure of the Ground," in the *Brahmayāmala*, the compendium of one hundred thousand verses. [Chapter 3] The Characteristics of the Image:
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme image, which is of six kinds.
It is born of stone, born of metal, born of gems, and auspicious with jewels.
Alternatively, it may be made of wood or clay, beautiful to behold,
provided with the height of the door and likewise the height of the base.
A wise man should have the smallest [liṅga] made as a replica of the embryo within the egg;
when divided into five parts, the middle-sized one shall consist of three parts.
Having made it equal to three times the womb-measure, two parts shall constitute the highest;
thus the fivefold likeness of the womb-measure is proclaimed.
One should fashion the image with a measurement of nine and a half *tālas* according to its characteristics;
and among these, the wise one should duly grasp the proportions.
The length of that [image] should be divided into three parts; each part shall constitute a separate image.
One part shall be the pedestal, determined as half of that [part].
Thus has the comfortable posture (sukhāsana) been described; it is to be performed by those standing in the proper sequence.
The seat for the comfortable posture should be square and elongated.
Having likewise made it square, one should arrange those respective parts;
on both sides, it is proclaimed to be rectangular.
Thus has the comfortable seat been described, endowed with its defining characteristics:
the head is five finger-breadths [in height], and the width of the face is one-third [of that].
The neck should be four finger-breadths [in width]; the heart is said to be the mouth.
The heart is located in the region of the navel, and the mouth is said to be in that very same place.
The genital organ should be five finger-breadths [in height], and the thighs should have two faces;
the shanks are said to be equal to the thighs, while the knower of proportions [should make] the single foot [of the pedestal].
The width of the chest-staff is twenty-five finger-breadths;
the hip-staff is said to be thirty finger-breadths in length and sixteen finger-breadths in width.
The length of the two forearms (bāhudaṇḍa) should be twenty-four finger-breadths (aṅgula),
and the length of the two lower arms (upabāhu) is said to be sixteen finger-breadths.
The face and the palm should be as wide as the wrist (one kalā);
both feet should be fourteen aṅgulas in length.
A wise man should divide the length of the hair into twelve parts;
the middle part of the trident should be four parts, and the upper part six parts.
(p. 6) It would be prescribed in the division of the *kaṭaśalkima* [sacrifice];
therefore, it has been stated that [the rule] applies according to the actual meaning, whereas the *vaktra* is measured by its syllables.
A trident should be made with white thread, and likewise a cloth for the month;
in the Kṛta age it should be white in color, and in the Tretā age it should indeed be red.
In the Dvāpara age it is yellow in color, while in the Kali age it becomes dark blue;
that which is white in appearance brings nourishment, and the red brings about increase.
Having made yellow the means for subjugation, black is said to be for the purpose of pacification;
the Goddess is supreme among women, therefore this is the highest honor.
Seated upon a white lotus, he is most excellent with knees reaching down to his ankles;
he has four arms and three eyes, and his head is adorned with a garland.
Adorned with various ornaments, her head is crowned by a garland of skulls;
she holds a trident in her right hand and a skull-cup in her left hand.
The right and left hands likewise grant the boons of granting wishes and fearlessness;
thus is the Great Hero to be visualized, adorned with all ornaments.
Wearing divine garments and a sacred thread, anointed with divine sandalwood paste,
with red eyes, large eyes, and red hair, he was enchanting to behold.
With red eyes and a red tongue, adorned with a red garland,
he holds in his right hands a sword, a khaṭvāṅga, a trident, and an axe.
One should place a skull, a bell, and hands holding petals and sprouts;
on the left, one should provide a bracelet while treading upon pieces of wood with the foot.
The three-eyed, boon-granting, and beautiful one is proclaimed as the Sole Hero;
he possesses two eyes of peace and is endowed with the radiance of his forehead.
Arising from the slaying of Dāruka, she is proclaimed as the one released from the forehead;
thus should the ritual be performed for the enchanting Ekavīrī.
One should place Raktākṣī in the east, Karālī in the south;
having placed Caṇḍākṣī in the west, one should place Mahocchiṣṭā in the north.
One should install Ambikā, Caṇḍikā, Ghorī, and likewise Ghoreśvarī in the corners, having performed the rite according to the procedure seen in the scriptures.
The Yoginī should have a yellowish complexion and be playful; she should be tawny.
These indeed should be placed in order as door-keepers at the location of the door.
The Yoginī should be known as the southern [image], and the Vilāsī should be the northern.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Rule for the Characteristics of Images," in the *Brahmayāmala*, the compendium of one hundred thousand verses. 3.
The Determination of Directions:
I shall now proclaim the determination of directions as condensed for the Kṣetrapāla.
Between the directions of Indra (East) and Īśāna (North-East), there should be the abode of the Kṣetrapāla.
Or a pedestal should be constructed there according to the prescribed procedure;
having dug into the ground there, one should act according to the rite as seen in the injunctions.
The best [measure] should be eight cubits, the middling four cubits, and the smallest half of that; thus it is proclaimed to be of three kinds.
Having relied upon a suitable site as desired, one should fashion the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha);
its front should first be prepared, endowed with the proper characteristics.
One should perform the excavation for the purpose of the pedestal according to its dimensions;
there, the wise one should cast the five jewels, both within and below.
The best of teachers, skilled in mantra, should insert nine syllables there—
five and one from elsewhere— into that [mantra] according to the sequence of its nine components.
Having thus laid out the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha) according to the rules, one should begin the work;
its height is declared to be equal to its width—such is its defining characteristic.
The wise one, having divided the height into three equal parts,
should first fashion a square base endowed with the proper characteristics.
First, the most wealthy [sacrificer] should have a square constructed there;
having divided that square into five parts, one of those parts should be further divided into three.
That [square], diminished by one part, is proclaimed as the circle-square;
having made the square equal, the square is placed above the circle.
There, a lotus should be fashioned, endowed with its characteristic marks;
one should make that lotus, possessing its characteristics, as one part out of three parts.
Its height has been stated to be exactly that; it should have eight petals and a pericarp.
Having thus constructed, in brief, this beautiful pedestal (pīṭha), one should proceed.
Or [he may worship] the Kṣetrapāla who brings pleasure to Śiva, according to his characteristics.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Kṣetrapāla," in the *Brahmayāmala-śatasahasra-saṃhitā*. 4.
9) The Planting of Sprouts:
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the planting of sprouts for every [rite].
And likewise during the sprinkling, the consecration, the festival, or the ritual bathing.
The fourfold vessel is prescribed for initiation, the commencement of the temple, likewise for the rite of the child-stage, and for the ritual of the auspicious sprout.
The conch, the shallow bowl, the small jar, and the vessel— these four types may be made of gold,
silver, copper, bell-metal, or even of clay.
It is proclaimed that in all yogas, each [of these] should be grasped as twelve [finger-breadths];
the conch-shaped [mark] of the conch is circular and eight finger-breadths in size.
Its width at the base should be half of that measurement;
at the tip, it should have the shape of a lotus petal, endowed with eight petals.
In that lotus, there should be the form of a conch; it is described as having the shape of a conch, with a length of sixteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas) and a width of three parts of that length.
His mouth is proclaimed to be the size of ten million insects;
his neck is three finger-breadths wide, and his belly is ten finger-breadths deep.
Its tail should have the form of a cow's ear; such is the characteristic of a conch.
A shallow bowl (śarāva) should be eighteen finger-breadths in height and free from cracks.
The face should be two *tāla*s in height, devoid of the black circle (*kṛṣṇamaṇḍala*);
it should be eighteen *aṅgula*s in length, and the *ghaṭikā* [of the nose] should be five and three [units].
The base should be six finger-breadths wide; in its center, the neck should be four finger-breadths.
The body of the jar (kumbha) should be eight finger-breadths in circumference, and its openings should be four finger-breadths.
The stalk of the *pālikā* is proclaimed to be one *aratni* in length;
its opening is sixteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in width.
For that purpose, the width of the throat is said to be half of that, and the cavity [the navel] is said to be half of that.
I shall describe the procedure for the pavilion in the rite of auspicious sprouts.
The wise one [should know] that the body of a Brāhmaṇa is ten cubits in width,
that of a Kṣatriya is nine cubits, and that of a Vaiśya is eight cubits.
The height of the rafters for Śūdras is proclaimed to be seven cubits;
it should have thirty-six pillars, sixteen pillars, or twelve pillars.
It is said to be eight cubits in length and likewise in its breadth;
having made it perfectly square and resembling the surface of a mirror.
Behind the two [shrines], one should construct a pavilion according to the prescribed rules, preceded by the proper rites;
it should be provided with four archways and adorned with banners in the eight directions.
A pavilion endowed with four doors and possessing the proper characteristics,
[surrounded] in sequence by the *vaṭa*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, and *lakṣa* trees and so forth.
One should have an archway constructed by them according to the prescribed rules, preceded by the proper rites;
it is declared to be five cubits in length and two cubits in width.
One should form the trident-shape with the hand raised upward and place the other hand on the ground;
[the colors] are white, red, black, smoky, and likewise the watery (vāruṇa).
One should place banners that are dark-blue, tawny, and yellow to the east;
and above, on the canopy, there should be a marvelous [banner] adorned with yak-tail whisks (*cāmara*) from its neck.
Then, having wrapped the pillars in succession with smooth garments made of dukūla, paṭṭa, and cotton,
they should subsequently be adorned even with sprouts.
One should worship the auspicious pavilion with incense, lamps, and fragrant scents;
having performed these rites first, one should then commence the rite of the sprouts (aṅkura).
Having smeared [the ground] with cow dung,
one should prepare its foundations with ten *droṇas* of rice, or half that amount, or half again.
Half a *droṇa* is the minimum; half of that again is for rice alone. One should scatter the heaps of rice to the right of these others.
One should have them made one cubit or three cubits in width, as is appropriate, and square in shape, following the proper sequence.
Having prepared a wise lotus-shaped seat,
and having first worshipped it with perfumes and flowers according to the prescribed ritual;
One should subsequently install the goddesses Raktā, Karālī, Caṇḍākṣī, Mahocchiṣṭā, and the others, starting with Śaṅkhā; then, having enclosed the area, one should fill it with soil.
One should worship the auspicious [seeds] with perfumes and other offerings beneath a canopy of mango sprouts;
thereafter, one should fill them with seeds, beginning with barley and following the prescribed order.
Barley, black gram, and horse-gram; bamboo shoots and cane shoots; rice, millet, apāmārga, śyāmāka, and niṣpāva.
Having taken sesame, mustard seeds, and mung beans— these thirteen seeds— according to what is available and in accordance with the place and time (p. 12).
Having washed [the vessels] with water and then likewise with cow's milk in succession,
one should offer betel leaf there for all the Mothers and Yoginīs.
Then the preceptor should especially cause betel-leaf to be offered;
the preceptor, whose self is purified, [should apply] pure fragrant unguents.
Wearing new garments, a turban, and an upper robe,
with a ring upon his hand, he is adorned with all ornaments.

Those who are excessively tall, those with a hump on the left side, those lacking eyes, the deaf, and those suffering from abdominal diseases— one should reject them during the scattering of parched grain.
Śipiviṣṭa should avoid one who is deformed or deficient in limbs;
he should accept one endowed with all auspicious marks, complete in every limb, and beautiful in every way.
By means of the Mātṛ-gāyatrī mantra, [he should honor] the reciters of the Brahmayāmala,
who are endowed with the ritual practices of all tantras.
Likewise, [there is] the teacher and the disciple, as well as censure...
One should abandon censure and the censure of one's family;
or, the knower of mantras should cause the seed-syllable to be sown with these [syllables] by means of the nine-syllable mantra.
With various Vedic chants, auspicious benedictions,
the resounding blasts of conchs and dundubhi drums, and the sounds of songs and musical instruments.
Or, the knower of mantras should have these [seeds] sown with the nine-syllable mantra;
the Guru should cause the seeds to be sown with the nine-syllable mantra.
One should sprinkle [the image] with water consecrated by reciting the Mātṛ-mantras,
and cover it individually with ten new, very fine cloths.
During the night, however, the Mātṛgāyatrī is recited with auspicious protections;
in that context, the preceptor is said to be the embodiment of the mantra.
One should cause the offering of oblations to the five deities beginning with Payodhi; one should cause the offering of oblations to those five deities, starting with Pāvaka.
Having done this, one should worship daily in this manner with flowers and other offerings. I shall now describe the offering of sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) according to the various distinctions of colors.
They were white, with the luster of silver, resembling elephants;
they were indeed yellowish-green, soft, and auspicious.
White in appearance brings all desired objects; silver-like in appearance bestows increase;
elephant-like in appearance brings wealth; and that which is beautiful and soft brings prosperity.
Gold has a golden luster; it brings about the increase of gold. Turmeric increases nourishment. Mṛddhanī bestows sons and grandsons, while Jīrṇatā is proclaimed [to have the opposite effect].
One should perform the cultivation of smoke, which destroys death and increases life;
likewise, one should employ the horizontal movement of wealth, measure by measure.
A black appearance portends expulsion; a smoky appearance brings about quarrels;
a blue appearance indicates the destruction of water, and untimely death will occur.
If it moves downward, there is the loss of one's gains; if it moves horizontally, it brings disease.
Therefore, with every effort, one should avoid all such inauspicious [signs].
One should sacrifice a single animal with the nine-syllable mantra;
for the sake of purification through expiation, one should perform a fire-oblation there according to the prescribed sequence.

O Brahmin, at the time of the offering of the sprouts (aṅkūrārpaṇa), one should cause the preceptor to offer all those seeds— one hundred and eight times— with the nine-syllable mantra. Indeed, the preceptor shall offer them.
Then, one should secretly deposit [the seeds] in the beautiful pavilion mentioned previously.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, on the Planting of Sprouts (*Aṅkurārpaṇa*), in the *Brahmayāmala-śatasahasra-saṃhitā*. 5.
The Installation. I shall describe the installation of the deities exactly and in due order,
whether in a village, a hellish place, a city, or even a small market town.
It bestows long life and health, increases wealth and grain,
brings about the increase of sons and grandsons, and results in abundance and prosperity.
In the center of the village is the excellent station of Brahmā with a new cloth;
likewise, there are the stations of Indra, Yama, the two Aśvins, and Śrī.
Between Indra and Agni is the supreme station of Vadha;
one should likewise designate the station of Kāma as being south of Sarasvatī.
Between the Āgneya and Yamya [directions] is the excellent station of the Pitṛs;
one should establish the Sāvitra [station] in the south and arrange the Yātudhāna [station] there as well.
Between the southern and southwestern directions, the station of Gaṇapati is said to be;
in the southwest is the station of Āsura, O fair-faced one— these are the nine deities.
The location for the Nāgas is prescribed in the southwest, in the western quarter, and in the center;
one should install Viṣṇu in the west and arrange the station of Lakṣmī there.
The station of Garuḍa is said to be between Nabhasvat and Varuṇa;
one should arrange the fire-offering (homa) in the north-west, which is called the station of the Gandharvas.
The place of Prajāpati is declared to be between Soma and the Maruts;
one should establish Vitteśa in the north and arrange Mārtāṇḍa there as well.
Between Soma and Śaṅkara is the wise Rudra, the eleventh;
and the station of Īśāna is Śaṅkara, accompanied by Śiva and Gaurī.
Between the Īśāna and Cakra [faces], the twelve Ādityas are said to reside; in the four directions beginning with the East, the station of Durgā is ordained.
In the centers of the villages, the Brahma-sthāna is ordained as the pericarp;
there one should worship the Mothers, honored with perfumes and flowers.
One should take nine jars, each with a lid and a wick,
along with cloth or new cloth, consecrated with the nine-syllable mantra.
Subrahmī, Māheśvarī, Kumārī, Vaiṣṇavī,
as well as Vārāhī, Māhendrī, and likewise Bhadrakālī.
One should place the seed-syllables of Agni along with those of Īśāna, beginning from the east;
there one should worship the boundary of the Goddess and perform the ritual according to the prescribed rule.
The preceptor should perform the fire oblation (homa) in sequence with the Vidyā-hṛdaya mantra; he should then commence [the ritual].
Having established [the deity] according to the ritual procedure, one should subsequently commence [the recitation].
One should establish it; the location for Jyeṣṭhā is prescribed in the northern quarter of the village.
In the northern directions of Jyeṣṭhā, the location of the fortress (koṭṭa) is prescribed;
this excellent fortress-monastery (koṭṭavyāśrama) should be constructed outside the village.
The station of the Mothers is ordained between Jyeṣṭhā and Avasava;
one may cause it to be constructed either in a village, in a city, or even at a crossroads.
One should install Viṣṇu in the western quarter and Śaṅkara in the northeastern quarter;
otherwise, for one who installs them incorrectly, there will be disease, grief, and fear.
One should predict famine, terrible strife, and total loss;
one must not perform [rituals] at the vital points (marmas) or during the middle of the path, and one should avoid piercing with cords.
One should prescribe the piercing according to the prescribed rite; however, one should indicate that death occurs from the piercing of the *araṇa*.
It is declared that piercing the trident causes pain from the trident, while piercing the six circles leads to destruction.
By piercing the vital points (marmas), one meets death; by piercing the tendons (rajju), there is destruction of the fetus;
by piercing the black [veins], there would be the ruin of the village; therefore, one should avoid these.
A village is defined as one endowed with a thousand Brahmins,
inhabited by the four castes, and comprising various ethnic groups.
One should know the city to be filled with wrestlers, actors,
and courtesans, as well as endowed with various castes of twice-born men.
A wise man should, according to the rules, establish a port that is inhabited by people of various mixed castes, provided with a residence for merchants, and crowded with traders.
That fortified city shall be equipped with the fourfold army, provided with gates and watchtowers,
and endowed with various kinds of precious gems.
O fair-faced one, a city (*nāgara*) should be twice the width of a village;
a town (*paṭṭana*) should be twice that of a city, and a market-town (*kheṭaka*) should be twice that of a town.
In this manner, O beautiful one, he should cause it to be performed according to the sequence of the ritual.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Installation of Deities," in the *Brahmayāmala*, the compendium of one hundred thousand verses.
The Ritual for Consecration:
O Brahmin, listen as I shall explain the ritual for consecration according to the proper sequence.
One should construct a square pavilion in front of the temple.
It is of three kinds— superior, middling, and likewise inferior—
and is endowed with four archways and adorned with four gates.
It is joined with sixteen pillars and measures ten or twelve cubits;
likewise, it may be joined with thirty-two pillars and measure sixteen cubits.
Or else, one may also construct a pavilion adorned with every kind of ornament.
It is joined with sixteen pillars and measures ten or twelve cubits;
likewise, it may be joined with thirty-two pillars and measure sixteen cubits.
It was encircled with *darbha* grass and garlands, hung with flower wreaths,
equipped with bells and chowries, and adorned with *kuśa*, *darbha*, and cowherd’s staffs.
The purifier (pavitra), joined with gold,
[measures] nine, five, or three finger-breadths (aṅgula) in length.
The stalk is said to be three finger-breadths long, and the knot should be one finger-breadth;
one should especially join it with the Mātṛgāyatrī mantra.
For one whose supreme [birth] was from an egg, the unmanifest [mantra] belongs to the divine language (*devagirā*).
[It should be performed] with vessels made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay if these are unavailable— provided they are unbroken, smooth, not cracked, and free from dark stains.
With water-pots of seasonal roots, even though they are wrapped with threads, provided with tufts of hair,
along with grains, and even though they are enveloped in cloths;
With these nine jars filled with pure water,
[one should place] rice, mung beans, millet, barley, and mustard seeds.
One should place the jars there, containing all fragrant substances;
one should set down the pitchers in the four directions, starting from the east, according to the proper sequence.
The knower of mantras, endowed with the five jewels and the nine-syllable mantra, (p. 19).
One should place the jar in the center; this is declared as the Vīreśī Tantra.
One should place Raktākṣī in the east and Karālī in the south.
One should assign Caṇḍākṣī to the west and Mahocchiṣṭhā to the north;
likewise, one should assign Ambikā, Caṇḍikā, Ghorā, and Aghoreśvarī.
In the corners, one should place water-pots according to the ritual prescribed in the scriptures,
using their respective seed-syllables conjoined with the nine-syllable mantra.
The wise one should place the water-pot (kalaśa) and display the trident mudrā;
he should then envelop it with perfumes, flowers, and the like, as well as with a pair of garments.
At the end of the vase, however, for each of the mantras in their proper order,
one should take an image of the Goddess made of either copper or sandalwood.
The form of the deity should be made stable and washed with pure water;
having honored it with a pair of garments, one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
One should place the *praṇava* (Oṃ) in the mind and place the *mūrti* (the form) in the mouth;
thereafter, one should place the nine-syllable mantra on the limbs of the image in due order:
in the mouth, the heart, the head, the navel, and the secret organ.
One should display the lotus mudrā on the chest and the feet;
having placed the heart [mudrā] on the heart, one should place the head [mudrā] on the head.
Having placed the *śikhā* [mantra] on the crest-lock, the *kavaca* on the body,
and the *astra* on the region of the hands, one should place the *netra* [mantra] upon the eyes.
The practitioner of mantras should place [the mudrās] on all limbs from the body of the Solitary Heroine:
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, and likewise Vaiṣṇavī.
One should place Vārāhī, Māhendrī, and Vīrabhadra, the lord of the Gaṇas,
as well as Ekavīrī upon the body using the single-mudrā (ekamudrā).
With a single-minded focus and firm vows, he should worship Vīrabhadra on the head and Gaṇādhyakṣa at the feet, each with their own respective mantra.
One should place Brahmāṇī on the face, Māheśvarī on the heart, Kaumārī on the anus, and Vaiṣṇavī on the navel mantra.
One should place Vārāhī at the waist and Jānā, who is Indrī, [therein];
one should place the entire world, both stationary and moving, in the belly.
One should assign the moon and sun to the eyes; one should assign the eyes to the forehead; having assigned the directions to the ears, one should assign space to the heart.
Having placed the earth upon his two feet, he should likewise arrange the three forms:
the gods, yakṣas, nāgas, kinnaras, and apsarases.
The wise one should place those [mantras] which have gone [to their respective locations] into the heart with their own respective mantras;
thus, by this procedure, the necklace and armlets are fashioned.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite, the preceptor should offer [the gift];
he should prepare a bed there, to the right of the water-pot (kalaśa).
On top of that,
the wise one should place, in sequence, cloths made of silk, wool, cotton, or blankets; then, with the limbs of the God of Gods, he should place [the seed-syllables] upon the eyes.
Having placed the *kūrca* (seat-grass) in that very place according to the prescribed characteristics, the wise one,
having thus performed the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*), should cause the solitary heroine (*ekavīrī*) to lie down according to the rite.
With the nine-syllable mantra accompanied by the word "jaya," the head should be placed toward the east; otherwise, it would be done at the feet.
One should place a cloth over the Goddess and Hara with the *īśas* (the directions), in pairs;
such a cloth may be used, or else one that is eye-like or even one that is *nirvāṇa*.
There, one should cause the food offering (nivedya) to be presented, accompanied by the recollection [of the deity].
Having touched [the disciples] with the water from the *kalaśa*, one should consecrate them with the Heart-mantra;
then, at the commencement of the fire-offering (*homa*), one should [consecrate] them all with all the mantras in their proper order.
By eight image-makers who possess the required characteristics,
who are skilled in the knowledge of mantras, pure, and devoted to the *Brahmayāmala*, according to the prescribed rule.
[The initiation should be performed] by those born of a lineage devoted to Śiva (pāraśaiva), who are endowed with the gaze of the Mothers,
and not by those who are deficient in limbs, nor the deaf, nor the blind, nor the deceitful.
One should perform the fire-oblation with *nāgavallī* leaves and hairs born from those of the same caste;
O Four-faced One, listen as I describe the characteristics of the preceptor.
One who is complete in all auspicious marks, a keeper of the conduct of the pledge,
an observer of the vow of Śakti, peaceful, free from physical defects, and free from disease.
The *Brahmayāmala* is supreme, knowing the ritual procedure for the Solitary Hero (*ekavīra*);
it is endowed with the practice of the *Mātṛtantra* and is expert in the *Mātṛtantra*.
One who knows the circle of the Mothers, whose realization proceeds from the investigation of the manifestation of Mātrā,
who is endowed with the purificatory rites of initiation, and who is most skilled in the sequence of consecration;
Born in an auspicious place, endowed with the rite of consecration,
knowing the procedure for the solitary hero (ekavīra), and auspiciously maintaining the vow of power (śakti).
With well-applied eyes and feet, free from dark circles,
red, with red lips, red palms, and wise.
Or one who speaks agreeably, who is devoted to the practice of the scriptures,
endowed with virtuous conduct and behavior, and free from attachment to worldly qualities.
He was endowed with virtues that were tranquil yet manifest, possessed of true prosperity,
marked by auspicious characteristics, and had tremulous, long eyes.
One whose feet are soft, who possesses a beautiful gait, and whose neck is auspiciously proportioned—
one endowed with such characteristics should always be appointed as a teacher according to the prescribed rule.
The bilva, the khadira, the palāśa, and the vaṭa;
the aśvattha, the udumbara, the padma, and likewise the śara.
The wise one should offer Apāmārga and Arka in sequence—one from each joint—into the Vāstu-homa. Therein, the most excellent of men should perform the oblation with Apāmārga.
The presiding priest of all the images should perform one hundred and eight oblations;
having offered twice that number for the preceptor, he should proceed in order with sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, and other materials.
One should perform one hundred and eight oblations for each of all the forms;
moreover, the wise practitioner should perform the oblations separately for the eight forms with their respective mantras.
One should perform the fire-oblation for the bearers of the forms with [the mantra] joined by the word *svatām*, endowed with nine syllables, and combined with the final vowel *sa*.
The Earth, Āpinī, Jīvā, Yaśasvinī, Khaḍginī, as well as Saurī, Candrī, and Pātnī— these are proclaimed as the eight forms (aṣṭamūrti).
The embodiment of those [elements] is at the head; the one who wards off the embodiment shall slay them.
First comes the worship of Earth, and then Water with the Vāruṇa [mantra].
Tejī is in the region of fire, Vāyavī in the domain of wind;
Khaḍginī is in the south-western quarter, and Saurī in the domain of Īśāna.
Having placed Candra in the north and Ahi in the south,
and having thus performed the placement according to the ritual rule, one should join [the deity] with the eight forms (aṣṭamūrti).
One should perform the fire-oblation for all the forms with their respective names;
one should offer the *avarga* in the east and the *kavarga* in the southeast.
The *ca*-group is in the region of Yama (the south), while the three groups beginning with *ta* are offered in the southwest;
the *ta*-group is in the western quarter, and the *pa*-group is in the domain of Vāyu (the northwest).
The *pavarga* [consonants] are in the region of Soma, while the *ṣavarga* [consonants] are in the domain of Īśa;
joined with all of these, the preceptor should commence the fire-oblation (*homa*).
As before, one should first install the world-protectors (lokapālas) in their proper order;
then, one should install the seven tongues [of fire] upon him in their respective places and according to sequence.
The third [section] of the eighth chapter is endowed with the defining characteristic;
the second [section] of the seventh chapter is endowed with the defining characteristic.
Endowed with the sixth vowel itself and beautifully adorned with a bindu on its head,
the tongue of many forms should be placed and directed toward the direction of the enemy.
The third [syllable] consists of seven parts and is joined with the second;
it is conjoined with the sixth and adorned with the bindu.
The tongue is like a silver vessel, and it is situated in the Saindra;
and in the second [section], there are eight other fragments, and this is the second [chapter].
Mounted by the sixth [vowel] alone, the parts of Indra [the letter 'i'] are arranged in sequence;
when joined with the Bindu above, the tongue becomes red.
Situated in the portion of Agni, she destroys the sins of those attached [to her];
she is the auspicious Mātīyā, the bestower of peace, belonging to the eighth Khaṇḍa.
But joined with the second of the seventh section,
conjoined with the sixth itself, and adorned above with the bindu.
The tongue named Kṛṣṇā is situated in the south-western direction;
she is beautiful with the primordial seed-syllables of the seventh section.
Furthermore, that which is joined with fire (R), endowed with the sixth vowel (Ū),
and conjoined with a bindu above, is the means for accomplishing all desires and goals.
Suprabhā, the beautiful tongue, is situated in the western direction;
she is the primordial seed-syllable of the seventh section and the bringer of auspiciousness.
Joined with the second [vowel] and conjoined with the sixth seed-syllable, and topped with the *bindu*,
she is the eternal increaser of victory.
The tongue situated in the northwestern direction becomes intensely red;
thus is the "Seven-Tongued" [Agni] described according to the rites seen in the scriptures.
In this manner, one should employ the sevenfold tongue in the fire-pit;
likewise, the best of instructors should employ the tongues upon the sacrificial mound.
Endowed with all of these, the preceptor should offer the mantra-oblation;
having offered fuel-sticks, he should touch his foot, and if he offers clarified butter, he should likewise touch it.
Having offered the *caru*, one should touch a drop; having offered sesame seeds, one should touch the fire;
having offered parched grain, one should touch the mouth and consecrate it with the *śūlamudrā*.
Afterwards, the wise practitioner should touch the syllables *kṛ*, *ga*, *kṣa*, *ra*, *spṛ*, *paścāt*, *kṣva*, *kā*, *ka*, and so forth;
having offered oblation after oblation, the mantra-master should touch [the body] from the feet up to the head.
Having touched heart with heart, one should place head upon head;
having touched the crest-lock, one should assign the armor to the space between the breasts.
The practitioner of mantra should touch the space between the breasts with all the mantras in their proper sequence;
having offered clarified butter there, he should likewise recite the heart-mantra and the others in due order.
With five oblations for each of the five [syllables], the wise one becomes the Moon by means of a sixth part;
having offered one hundred oblations with the nine-syllable mantra, he becomes a solitary hero.
The fourfold form consists of four oblations, while the eightfold form consists of eight;
for the twelve sages, it is said that there are twelve oblations.
One should offer sixteen oblations for the sixteen forms;
for the thirty-two forms, thirty-two oblations are prescribed.
That which is to be offered for their fulfillment should be joined with the words of their own names;
having offered ten oblations to the Yoginīs, one should offer five times to the retinue.
Having thus offered the oblation according to the prescribed rule, the wise man should sprinkle the house with water;
having sprinkled it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), he should do so while reciting the nine-syllable mantra.

One should sprinkle the outer and inner [areas], as well as the retinue and the planets, with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya); thereafter, one should begin the installation. At the time of the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana), one should sacrifice seven animals.
One should offer blood, flesh, and bone as a homa-oblation with the root mantra.
Then one should offer the bali-oblation to the directions and arrange it with blood and meat,
accompanied by the sounds of conchs, kettledrums, and other instruments, as well as ḍamaru drums and trumpets.
Accompanied by the sounds of the *mātṛ* hymns and the tumultuous beating of drums and kettledrums,
one should cause joy there with dances, songs, and so forth during that circumambulation.
For this is declared to be the Brahma-rite of formal acceptance;
when an auspicious hour has arrived at dawn, the installation shall take place.
One should first arrange the jewels and so forth, and afterwards begin the ritual installation.
These include gems, metals, grains, seeds, and likewise medicinal herbs.
O Brahmin, one should place them in sequence according to the ritual prescribed in the scriptures:
the diamond, the emerald, the pearl, and the ruby.
Vaiḍūrya, puṣparāga, indranīla, pravālaka,
gomedaka, and māṇikka are proclaimed as the nine gems (navaratna).
By means of the nine-syllable mantra, according to the sequence starting from the east,
[one should offer] gold, silver, copper, iron, tin, and lead.
And having ascended, one should sequentially place the extensive [elements] starting from the east:
Haritāra, Gañjaka, Mākṣira, and likewise Guṇapīta.
One should place Saurāṣṭra, Gairika, and likewise Vajragandha,
in sequence starting from the east, using the nine-syllable mantra.
One should place sesame, mustard seeds, mung beans, rice, niṣpāva beans,
barley, black gram, and millet with the nine-syllable mantra.
Lakṣmī, sahadevī, viṣṇukrānti, bala, garikā,
jīvavallī, vāhrī, and pāksava are the moving [plants].
One should perform the sequential placement (*vinyāsa*) upon the two [mandalas] using the nine-syllable mantra;
one should have a nine-compartmented [mandala] fashioned, beautifully adorned with copper.
The practitioner of mantras should place the station of Brahmā and should not effect any unification;
likewise, he should place the tortoise, the earth, the conch, and the lotus leaf.
The vajra, the trident, the mace, and likewise the sword— these,
when joined with the mere recollection of the nine-syllable mantra, [grant success].
One should place the seed-syllables, the paths, the colored powders, the medicinal herbs, and the metals;
first, one should place the Brahma-sthāna, which is auspicious and bestows long life and health.

Having thus performed the ritual placement according to the rule, one should smear [the image] with milk-rice porridge on an auspicious day and at a favorable moment, accompanied by the sounds of conch shells and kettledrums.
The preceptor should duly install the Brahma-sthāna and the Kautuka,
using the kūṭākṣara together with nine seed-syllables (bījas) joined with nine syllables.
Within a short moment, one should perform the rite of establishing [the deity] in an upright posture;
then, having offered the *arghya*, the mantra-practitioner should be devoted to the visualization of the Hero (*vīra*).
There, one should indeed sacrifice animals for the sake of stability during the Kālikā rite;
or, with the sacrificer at the head, one should perform the rite with mantras and ladles (darvī) accompanied by his sons.
Having thus consecrated the *kavituka* according to the rite, one should establish it;
having set aside the portion for the deity, one should perform the ritual recitation (*carcā*) dedicated to Brahmā.

One should cause [the disciple] to enter after he has been joined with the recollection [of the deity], having performed the recitation three times with the nine seed-syllables of Kṛtākṣara, which are also endowed with nine syllables.
Having offered the *arghya* there itself, one should cause Bhadrakālī to enter;
then, having meditated upon the *sakala* (manifest) and *niṣkala* (unmanifest) forms, one should again install the goddesses.
Then one should invoke the Goddess, who is of terrifying form and carries a skull-cup,
accompanied by a trident, a sword, a khaṭvāṅga staff, and a shield.
Holding a bell and a hand-drum, as well as a serpent-noose, the goddess wears a garland of severed heads; she has three eyes and blood-red lotuses.
She is dark-complexioned, very firm, and indeed Raudrī, higher than the highest;
she is joined by all the hosts of bhūtas and pretas, as well as by the hosts of the Mātṛ-yonis.
p.
29) With all these [mantras] for those who have been humiliated, the wise one should invoke the Goddess—
she who is inconceivable, supreme, subtle, unmanifest, imperishable, and compassionate.
The Great Goddess Maheśvarī, the womb of the world of manifold forms, whose body is the universe,
the goddess with many faces and many hands.
She possessed many forms, was dark as clarified butter, and had many noses;
she was endowed with many ears and possessed many breasts.
The best among those who know the tantras should install her who is endowed with many faces, adorned by the ocean as her garment, and whose limbs are variegated with the [ornaments of] Indra.
Having sprinkled [the deity] with water from the ritual jar (kalaśa), one who knows the mantras should install his own form and likewise install the retinue with their respective mantras.
Having sprinkled [the body] with divine water, one should then perform the deposition of the vowels and consonants;
then, having worshipped it according to the prescribed rule, one should offer the body.
Milk-rice, kṛsarā-rice, yellow rice, and rice with jaggery;
pure rice combined with ghee, and [food] accompanied by curd, honey, and ghee.
Edibles, foods, drinks, things to be licked, and likewise things to be sucked; *baulaka*, *maṇḍaka*, *pūrikā*, and *ghṛtaka* as well.
Honey, meat, liquor, molasses, flour, and likewise honey—
thus the Goddess may become threefold when joined with a hundred thousand portions of meat.
One should especially offer many *kādaka* vessels of water for the *arghya* oblation;
then one should present the directional offering (*diśābali*) consisting of meat combined with parched grain (*lāja*).
One should properly honor the preceptor with cows, gold, and other gifts;
this is declared in the ritual for consecration as the cause for bringing peace to the kingdom.
In the inner sanctum, however, the wise man should have seven compartments constructed;
having installed [the deity] there, he should worship it with wealth.
Having established the deity of the permanent image (dhruvārcā) in the portion for battle, the knower of tantra best, being the self of all beings, should offer the piśāca portions to the piśācas.
Thus, the threefold document [should be prepared] preceded by the prescribed ritual.
This concludes the seventh chapter, titled "The Procedure for Consecration," in the *Brahmayāmala*, the compendium of one hundred thousand verses.
Henceforth, I shall explain the ritual of Nyāsa according to the sequence of the rules.
Nyāsa is said to be of three kinds, which accomplish all desired aims.
The distinction between emanation and withdrawal, as well as the placement for maintenance,
is proclaimed as the "emanation placement" (sṛṣṭinyāsa), extending from the crown of the head down to the feet.
The placement from the feet up to the head is the dissolution-placement (saṃhṛti-nyāsa) arising from Bhava;
that which is from the nose up to the heart is called the maintenance-placement (sthiti-nyāsa).
First, one should perform the bath with water, and after that, the bath with clay;
thereafter, the practitioner of meditation and yoga should perform the ritual of the bath through recitation.
One should assume the lotus posture (padmāsana) with the hands in the añjali-mudrā;
first, one should perform the inhalation (pūraka), for Brahmā is the presiding deity therein.
The *kumbhaka* [breath-retention] is situated in the center of the heart, a region illumined as partless (*niṣkala*).
It is the partless Supreme Power (*paramāśakti*), fully endowed with the seat of the mantra.
Having meditated upon the forms of Kālī, Karālī, Virālī, and likewise Mālinī, in due order within the center of the heart-lotus.
Thereafter, one should perform the placement of the fingers on the hands (karāṅgulīnyāsa) together with the *nirmalākṣa* [mudrā],
making it equal to a "serpent-hand" (*nāgahasta*) and endowed with the *maṇimaṇḍa*.
The right thumb is Brāhmī, while the index finger is Maheśvarī;
the middle finger is Kaumārī, and the ring finger is Vaiṣṇavī.
One should place Vārāhī on the little finger of the right hand;
on the left hand, one should place Indrāṇī beginning with the little finger.
One should place Cāmuṇḍā on the ring finger, Vīrabhadra on the middle finger,
Mahāvighna on the index finger, and Karālī on the thumb.
In this manner, one should perform the sequence of emanation, and immediately thereafter the sequence of withdrawal;
beginning with the left thumb, one should deposit [the mantras] into the nine powers.
One should place Śāntī on the thumb; one should place Soṇī on the index finger;
one should make Khaḍvāṅgī the middle finger; and Anāmī is indeed the nose.
One should place the little finger upon the tip of the beautiful [forefinger] established at the end;
having placed the little finger like a pearl, one should then place the index finger at its tip.
For the wrathful [deity], having placed the thumb, the placement is proclaimed as "sthiti" (stability).
Having placed the syllable *praṇava* on the fingers, one should place the syllable *phaṭ* on the index finger (*tarjanī*).
The syllable *phaṭ* is on the middle finger, the syllable *phaṭ* is on the ring finger,
and the syllable *huṃ* is on the little finger; this is called the form of the little finger (*kaniṣṭhākāra*).
One should place the syllable *phaṭ* in the middle finger of the many-armed [deity],
and place the white *huṃ* syllable upon the thumb of that index finger.
One should place Caṇḍī Raudrī at the middle of the right hip,
and one should place Caṇḍī Raudrī at the middle of the left [hip].
One should place Bhairavī there in the center of the jewel on the left;
Bahuvīra on the right and Ekavīra on the left.
One should place the *arka* mantra on the back of the palms joined together;
this is declared to be the *karanyāsa*, and after this follows the *mahānyāsa*.
One should place the *praṇava* on the head; Brahmā is the presiding deity there. At the syllable *kha*, the forehead should be placed; Skanda is the presiding deity there.
The syllable *va* is in the middle of the mouth, with Vighna as its presiding deity;
the syllable *ma* is in the center of the heart, with Durgā as its presiding deity.
One should place the syllable *bha* there upon that person, the deity who is the essence of truth;
thus is the Great Seal of Emanation (*sṛṣṭimahāmudrā*), which is called the ritual placement of emanation (*sṛṣṭinyāsa*).
Having placed the syllable Oṃ at the two feet, the Earth is the presiding deity there;
and having placed the syllable Jre in the middle of the knees, Durgā is the presiding deity of the threads.
Having placed the syllable *Dreṃ* as fire, Umā is the presiding deity there;
then the syllable *Hreṃ* is at the front of the breast, and Śrī is the presiding deity there.
The syllable *hroṃ* is placed on the two arms, with Jyeṣṭhā as its presiding deity;
the syllable *hreṃ* is the placement for the eyes, with Sarasvatī as its presiding deity.
One should perform the placement (nyāsa) with the syllable *phaṭ* on the region of the shoulders, for which the presiding deity is [Skanda];
and likewise, one should place the syllable *huṃ* on the back, for which the presiding deity is Pāli.
One should place the letter *ha* in the heart; its presiding deity is Nāda-śakti.
The placement (*nyāsa*) of these [letters] is performed with the fist-mudrā and the bindu-mudrā.
One should place Vīrabhadra upon the head with the mantra;
above that, one should place the devotee in the form of meditation.
One should place the obstacle-mantras from the forehead upward,
and there, at the end of the four squares, one should place Brahmāṇī with the root-mantra.
Likewise, above the mantra is she who has four faces and four arms.
Having meditated thus with the mind, one should install Brahmāṇī there;
Māheśvarī is established in the middle of the mouth by means of her mantra.
Above that, one should place the goddess Kaumārī, who has four arms and three eyes, at the tip of the ear by means of her root mantra.
Above the mantra, one should perform the placement of Kāmārī, who has four arms;
one should place Vaiṣṇavī with the root mantra both externally and internally.
One should perform the placement (vinyāsa) above the mantra; likewise, one should place Vaiṣṇavī and Ekahastinī, and with the root mantra, one should place Vārāhī at the heart.
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon his mantra; Vārāhī, four-armed, is established in the center of the navel by means of the root-mantra of Indrāṇī.
Upon its center is the placement of Indrāṇī, who holds a thunderbolt in her hand;
Cāmuṇḍī is established in all the limbs by means of the root mantra.
Having meditated upon Cāmuṇḍā of fierce appearance above that mantra,
and having thus meditated on the world as consisting of the Mothers, one proceeds with the sacrifice.
It is both with parts and without parts, and it is both without parts and with parts and without parts;
the gross body, however, follows its controller according to its capacity, just as a great chariot follows its driver.
In the same way, the aggregate of the senses follows the mind alone;
just as a snake trembles again and again upon seeing Tārkṣya.
Seeing a worshipper who is without mantras, one trembles with a surge of joy for Śiva;
through the union with the instruction of Śiva, this is here called "Śiva’s delight."
One born in a Pāraśava family, having performed a special bath,
should undergo a haircut, purification of the teeth, a ritual bath with mantras, and anointing with unguents.
He wears a turban and a sacred thread, with a pure cloth as an upper garment;
he is adorned with earrings and a golden ring for his finger.
A beautiful rosary made of coral, pearls, and rudrākṣa beads,
as well as the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) and especially anointing with sandalwood paste.
The *bherikā*, the *poṣaṇa*, and the *pāraśava* are thus remembered;
they are employed during the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), and at the time of the *utsava* offering (*balikāla*).
At the commencement of the initiation with the rosary, and likewise in the station of the Child (Bāla),
one should strike the drum in sequence as soon as the ritual action has begun.
If the drum lacks its handle, the king and his kingdom perish;
likewise, if it is otherwise [defective], the king and his kingdom perish.
For the purpose of pacifying those defects, one should employ the seven purifications;
accompanied by food and water for the feet, this should be proclaimed in all ritual acts.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Nyāsa," in the Śrī Brahmayāmala, the compendium of one hundred thousand verses. || 8 ||
The pedestal.
Now I shall describe in due order the characteristics of the offering pedestal (*balipīṭha*).
This [pedestal] rising from the base in the main temple is the extent of the *bhūtapīṭha*.
It should be outside the foot, or in the middle, or even inside the foot;
its width should be one and a half times its height.
Having likewise increased the height of the pedestal (pīṭha) by one-quarter,
if the measurement from the base of the fire-offering (homa) up to the pericarp (karṇikā) consists of thirty-two parts, it is correct.
The height of the *kumuda* is said to be one part of the *bhūta* (five parts), and the *kampaka* is said to be one part [of the same];
the height of the *caraṇa* is six parts, or it may be the *kampaka* consisting of a portion of Śiva.
One should place the Mahāpadma at one-sixteenth part [of the height], the elevation of the lotus at one-fourth part,

Alternatively, listen to the rule for measuring the door in another way:
the height of the architrave (hāra) should be one *tāra* less by one-quarter, or two-quarters.
One should perform the previously mentioned procedure for the superior, inferior, and middling types, as well as for the *tuṅga* [type],
up to the *karṇikā* of the fire-offering (*homa*), numbering twenty-eight.
The height of the pedestal (upāna) or the neck (kala) shall be one-sixth of the measurement;
the height of the dome (kumbha) shall be five parts, and the height of the neck (kaṇṭha) is said to be one part.

the kampamūrdhva should be one-ninth, and the mehapatti one-twelfth, or specifically one-eighth.

Having placed the portion of the Vedas as the petals and the portion of Śiva as the arising of the pericarp, one should place the syllable of the pedestal at the end of the four ages; this is the body of the partless (niṣkala) [deity].
One should know the self (ātman) as abiding and complete; it becomes moved when [the vital breath] departs. Life-force (āyuḥ) is thus fully described, and it is perceived by the self.
The field is taught by me through its various distinctions according to the form of the field;
it is like oil situated within sesame seeds, or as milk is certain to exist within [the udder].
They say the field is like sesame seeds, and the oil is said to be the field; beyond these two there is nothing else, which should be understood as all-pervading like space.

The *mātṛkā* is called the field (*kṣetra*), while the Lord is called the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*). The imperishable supreme support is called the object of support (*adheya*) and is termed power (*śakti*).
It is said that there is no self; rather, that self is Bhairava.
Mantra is the Supreme Power (Parāśakti), and Power is called Bhairava.
Bhairava is born from Bhairava, and he is to be discerned within that Śakti;
otherwise, the deity Śakti is that which has arisen within the Bhairavas.

thus, O Brahman, one becomes Śakti, and beyond that is Brahmaśakti.
One should not perform the initiation of the Mother (mātṛdīkṣā), nor the ritual sequence (krama), nor the worship (arcana) here.

One should discard the oil, impurities, and the tooth-stick in a clean place;
having washed one's hands and feet, one should then prepare the tooth-stick.
Having touched water and become pure therein through bathing, he who has attained the state of a Śaiva should take earth with his left hand and perform the act of scattering it.
O Lord, the practitioner, for the sake of destroying obstacles, should offer the oblation with the three-part mantra, using the terrible face itself as the mantra.
One part should be for the directions and one part for the water;
having gathered these and drawn [the diagram], one should perform the bath for oneself according to the prescribed sequence.
The Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, the Kojinī, the Kāṇṭhakī,

likewise cause all meritorious sacred sites to abide within these waters for you both.
One should first recite the Gaṅgāhrada mantra, and afterwards one shall attain the most excellent purification;
for that which is the Śiva-tīrtha is more purifying than all other holy places.
Having formed a full añjali, one should place it upon the head;
there, one should meditate upon the supreme Īśāna like a submerged staff.
Having emerged from the water, one should subsequently recollect Sadyojāta;
then, having stepped out from the midst of the water, one should sit facing north.

then, having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), one should meditate upon Śiva in the heart.
From cessation (nirodha) wind is born; from wind, fire is born;
even that which is called heat is born [from it], and thereafter internal purity is said to arise.
Once the exterior and interior have been purified, one should perform the *śivahasta* rite;
thereafter, O twice-born one, one should make oneself Śiva, endowed with the three principles (*tritattva*).
Having sipped water there, one with a *kūrca* in hand should touch water and satisfy the gods, the sages, and the ancestors in their proper order.
When the path of meditation is completed,
it is prescribed for the practitioner that he first perform a water-bath and then a bath with ashes according to the proper sequence.
Having carefully collected white, red, black, and tawny cow dung in due order according to age, one should consecrate it with the mantra *Oṃ*.
Having established the syllable *na*, one should gradually purify the syllable *ma*.
Having formed the fist with the syllable *śi*, one should gradually purify the syllable *va*.
The practitioner of the rite should burn the syllable *ya* with fire and the syllable *oṃ*;
having thus reduced it to ashes, he should then perform the rite of consecration once again.
One should place the vessel there and burn it gradually with fire;
then, having recited the five-syllable mantra, one should perform the collection of another vessel.
One should cause [the offering] to be given with fragrant flowers upon a pure spot,
constantly touching the southern [direction], which is the supreme seed-syllable of Amṛtasva.
Having been initiated, one should daily worship that supreme destroyer of all sins,
according to the sequence of the initiation of knowledge, the initiation of austerity, and the initiation of mantra.
The initiation of knowledge is for Brahmins, the initiation of austerity is for the king (Kshatriya),
the initiation of mantra is for the Vaishya, and likewise for the Shudra as well.
Nor should one cause members of other castes, such as Śūdras and likewise others of various classes, to perform work that is appropriate for [the higher] castes.
The initiation (dīkṣā) must be performed according to the prescribed sequence after having propitiated the Guru;
O Rudra, he whose father and mother are the fire is one who has been initiated as a worshiper.
For that person born of a noble lineage, having abandoned his former births,
he is like a gem upon a mandala, an altar, or even on crystal.
One should have [the deity] made on a wall, on a painted cloth, or even within the heart;
or the practitioner, whose self is the *piṇḍa*, should worship or perform meditation upon it.
The student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and the mendicant;
and the Śaiva, the Pāśupata, and the Soma— these are the three Siddhāntas.
One should likewise imagine the east, the south, the west, and the north,
as well as the zenith above, as being connected to Īśāna.
The form of Īśāna is in the east, and Īśvara is in the south;
the form of Brahmā is in the west, and likewise Śiva is in the north.
Above that is Sadāśiva; these five forms are in this sequence. Through each respective face, one should worship the corresponding state during initiation.
One whose body is smeared with ashes should daily worship Brahmā, who sequentially presides over creation, maintenance, and dissolution, through his various manifestations.
Having completely renounced all attachments, one should gradually cultivate the sense of oneness;
and one should worship Viṣṇu daily through recitation, fire-offerings, ritual acts, and so forth.
It is said that for the householder in particular, it takes the form of a lamp;
and for all those who have been initiated, O men and women, it is performed with great devotion.
The Tripuṇḍra should be applied by measuring three finger-breadths;
indeed, it should be three finger-breadths in circumference for everyone without exception.
Having worshipped specifically according to this very sequence of ritual injunctions,
one born of the Kula should meditate upon oneness therein and thus attain perfection.

I shall describe the daily worship which destroys the sins of the day.
Having heard this "Peace of the Village," which destroys enemies and Rākṣasas,
it serves to increase longevity, prosperity, and sons, and to augment wealth and grain.

Having performed the ritual bath with mantras, and thereafter the ash-bath (bhasmasnāna),
the practitioner, facing north, should perform meditation.

having worshipped them in due order according to the rule with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
Or she may stand at the door of the Yoginīs; through bathing, she takes on the form of fire.

Vijayī and Jṛmbhiṇī—these two are the door-yoginīs;
the wise one should worship them with incense, flowers, and other offerings, using their own names.
Śuddhinī is in the eastern region, while Sukeśinī is in the southeast;
Viṣukaṇṭhī is in the south, and likewise Sundarī is in the southwest.
In the west is the goddess Jāvalī; in the northwest is Koṭarākṣasī;
in the north is the goddess Tadarśinī; and in the northeast is Śatrumardinī.
Daṇḍakuṇḍodarī, Bhīmī, Kīḍī, Vijayavinyayā, Vyālāmukhī, Virūpākṣī, Rājadevī, and Raśakti.
Nīlakeśī, Vikarṇī, and likewise Vyālakeśī;
O Goddess, Ugrapaiśācinī and Vetālī by name.
Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, and Varuṇa;
likewise Vāyu, Soma, and Īśāna; and Śaṅkarī in the north (Kauberyāṃ).
Vighneśa and Vīrabhadra, as well as Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, and Indrāṇī.
And likewise Cāmuṇḍī— having worshipped each of these Mothers by their respective names with their corresponding Gāyatrī mantras in due order.
Brahmāṇī is with Śuklavāsa and Vīra, both dressed in white;
Īśvarī is dressed in white, while Kumārī is dressed in garments of the Sindhu river.
Vaiṣṇavī is clad in yellow garments, Vārāhī in black garments,
Indrāṇī in fine silk, and Cāmuṇḍī in red garments.
Vighneśa is [represented by] a sword; indeed, a garment is prescribed for each [deity].
Hirivera is the face, and Brahmāṇī is said to be the fragrance.
Īśvarī possesses the scent of māṃsī, Kaumārī likewise possesses saffron (kuṅkuma),
Vaiṣṇavī possesses royal musk (rājakastūrī), and Vārāhī possesses niryāsa.
One should worship Ārdramēṣa, Indrāṇī, Cāmuṇḍī, red sandalwood,
white sandalwood for the unguent, and likewise Vīravighna.
One should likewise worship Gaṇeśa with ketakī and jasmine flowers;
Vīrabhadra with karavīra, and Brahmāṇī with white lotuses.
Śvetārka and Īśvarī, Kaumārī and Kumuda,
Vaiṣṇavī and Tulasī, as well as Vārāhī and Mallikā.
Jāti flowers for the Śūdras, a red lotus for Cāmuṇḍā,
guggulu resin for Vīrabhadra, and white flowers for the Four-faced One (Caturmukha).
Īśvarī [offers] agarwood, Kaumārī devadāru wood, Vaiṣṇavī forest incense, and Vārāhī clarified butter incense.
Indrāṇī, Caturniryāsa, Cāmuṇḍī, Jātudhūpaka,
Vighneśa, Agaru, Śītārī, and all the deities.
The mantra for fragrance is for the fragrance, the mantra for flowers is for the flowers;
the mantra for incense is for the incense, and the mantra for lamps is for the lamps.
One should recite the respective root-mantra of each [deity] in sequence with its corresponding *gāyatrī* mantra;
having invoked each respective image, one should worship it in due order.
One should offer pure rice to Vīrabhadra and to Vighneśa;
one should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) to Brahmāṇī and kṛsara-rice to Īśvarī.
Kaumārī receives rice with turmeric, Vaiṣṇavī rice with jaggery,
Vārāhī rice with black gram, and Indrāṇī rice with mung beans.
One should offer red rice and sesame rice to Cāmuṇḍī;
having recited the food-offering mantra, one should present each of these in that manner.
I shall now describe each [deity] individually; listen, O Four-faced One!
Vighneśa and Vīrabhadra, as well as the sacrificial fuel and bilva wood, are likewise explained.
Brahmāṇī is associated with the Palāśa tree, and likewise Āheśvarī with the Arka;
Kaumārī is associated with the Audumbara, and Vaiṣṇavī with the Aśvattha.
Vārāhī is likewise from the Plakṣa tree, Indrāṇī from the Khadira, and Cāmuṇḍī from the Nyagrodha; these are proclaimed as the sacrificial fuel (samidh) for those deities.
I shall now describe separately each of those [woods] for which fuel-sticks (samidh) are offered;
however, if even these are unavailable, palāśa wood may be used for all offerings.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Worship of the Mothers," in the *Brahmayāmala*, the compendium of one hundred thousand verses.
[Now follows] the Fire Ritual (*agnikārya*). Hereafter, I shall fully explain the sequential procedure for the fire ritual.
Furthermore, the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) or the fire-pit (kuṇḍa) for the fires is of two kinds.
The triangle, the half-moon,
the square, the circle, the hexagon, the lotus, the octagon, and the pentagon, in due order.
The quadrangular *kṛtī* fire-pit accomplishes all desired aims;
the *yoni*-shaped pit brings about the prosperity of progeny, and the half-moon shape destroys enemies.
A hexagon is said to bestow tranquility; a circle is for the sake of rain;
a hexagon brings an increase in crops; and a lotus-shaped figure is for the sake of victory.
The eight-cornered [pit] is to be known as bestowing nourishment, while the five-cornered one destroys disease;
thus the fruit of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) has been stated, and now the altar-ground (sthaṇḍila) is described.
One should have [the altar] made in a pit or on a leveled mound, measuring one cubit;
one should construct three tiers (mekhalā), measuring four, three, and two finger-breadths [respectively].
The girdle (*mekhalā*) below [the waistband] should have a height of two finger-breadths;
however, the middle girdle should have a width of three finger-breadths.
The girdle should be four finger-breadths high and its lower edge [should be] hidden;
one should fashion the navel at six finger-breadths, toward the west or the south.
With a navel like a leaf of the *aśvattha* tree and measuring one finger-breadth,
one should smear the ground with cow dung and sweep it with *darbha* grass while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
If the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is to be purified, it should undergo cleansing, washing, drying,
heating, and sprinkling by means of the five Brahmans beginning with "Sadyojāta."
Having taken a piece of earth from a non-saline place and sprinkled it with water, one should cast it toward the north;
it should be made one cubit wide using dry sand from a pure location.
It should be three finger-breadths in height, with a level surface that is neither too low nor too high;
there should be three lines starting from the eastward-pointed end, and two of them should have their tips pointing toward the north.
The central thread belongs to Brahmā, while Vaiṣṇavī is on the right;
Kālī shall be the northern thread—these are proclaimed as the presiding deities.
The presiding deities of the three lines with their tips pointing eastward have been proclaimed:

But previously, the presiding deities of the forms of Yoga have been proclaimed;
having drawn [the lines], one should prepare the fuel with three [lines] pointing eastward and one [line].
One should draw three lines— the middle, the southern,
and the northern— and having marked the northern one with upward lines, one should discard the sacrificial fuel.
Having understood this written mantra as well as the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra),
[one should know that] the best [fire-drill] is produced from sun-crystal (sūryakānta), while that made of wood would be middling.

having placed it before the patient and sprinkled it with the Bahurūpī mantra.

then, having cast fuel into the fire in another location of the fire-god, [one should proceed].
Having meditated upon Vāgīśī in the center of the navel— possessing the luster of a blue lotus petal and seated upon a *kūrca* of seasonal flowers— one should do so by means of her root mantra.
In a sacrificial pit consecrated with mantras, one should invoke Vāgīśī, the mother of fire, and Vāgīśvara, the father; having established them there, one should worship them.
Three-eyed and four-armed, with a luster like that of a ruby,
he grants boons and fearlessness, holding a trident and a noose in his hands.

then, recollecting the seed-syllable of fire (*vahnibīja*), one should deposit it through the path of the *yoni*.

then, having placed the fire upon the ground at the knees by way of the womb-path (yonimārga), [one should proceed].
Recalling "Hraṃ" and hearing [the invocation], he should say, "Oṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to Agni," and having taken fuel for the fire, he should cause the fire to be well-kindled in three ways.

Having worshipped with scents, flowers, and rice grains, one should offer three oblations;

One should worship the fire with the *Hṛdaya-mantra*; this is known as the *puṃsavana* rite.
In the *puṃsavana*, one should offer a flower and three oblations of sesame seeds.

The invocation and other rites, the immediate food offering, its specific mudrās and so forth,

Raktākṣī, Kālī, Caṇḍākṣī,
and likewise Ucchiṣṭeśvarī— these and others should be strewn around as the presiding deities.
One should spread [the grass] with the tips pointing north from east to west,
and one should spread it with the tips pointing east from south to north.

the *brahmāsana* is on the south, and the vessel-seat (*sthālyāsana*) is on the west.

then Vāṇī and Vāgīśvarī, and after that, the dismissal (udvāsana).
The *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, the vessel for clarified butter, the *praṇītā* water-vessel, and likewise the *prokṣaṇī*;
the fuel-sticks, the *kūrca* grass-bundle, the *caru* oblation, the *darvī* spoon, the *sirī*, and the water-pot.

one should prepare the pairs of vessels with their openings facing downward.
Having taken the *prokṣaṇī* vessel, one should fill it with water;
taking a piece [of grass] one span (*vitasti*) long, one should place it in the middle of that [vessel], tied with a knot.
With the thumb and ring finger, perform the splashing of water;
having sprinkled the vessels with consecrated water while reciting the *varman* mantra.
The *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, fuel and other such items, and golden materials are placed on the right;
likewise the sacrificial wood (*samidh*), clarified butter (*ājya*), cooked rice (*caru*), parched grain (*lāja*), mustard, barley, and sesame.
Mudga beans, bamboo shoots, the leaf of the śrī tree, the fruit of the plantain, goat’s flesh and blood, fish, and liquor combined together.

turn upward the vessels for the substance-oblation, such as the *caru* and others.
