Having specifically slaughtered an animal according to the sequence beginning with the Brāhmaṇas,
one should not cause the slaughter of animals for other castes as well.
If cutting occurs in that very place, the king and his kingdom perish;
one should perform an expiation and again undertake a rite of pacification.
One should then cut that [image], which is complete with all the primary marks, beautiful in all its limbs,
and endowed with such characteristics.
The practitioner should strike it on the neck and offer its blood;
if one remains there with a fixed gaze, one should perform the appropriate expiation.

Furthermore, the knower of mantras should offer an animal sacrifice there, beginning with water and ending with the *ūdīraka* oblation; having performed the *homa*, he should do so for the pacification of that defect.
There, the wise one should cause a mandala to be made; he should draw it with three colors, making it square on the outside and beautifully adorned with a trident.
Having drawn an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp in the center,
one should indeed worship the Mothers there with perfumes, flowers, and incenses.
Having placed nine jars together with their lids and strainers,
they should be joined with colored threads according to the respective signs and consecrated with the nine-syllable mantra.
Having established the Vyoma and the Pāraśava, there are four [stages], including the fourteenth;
as well as the initiation of the Mothers (mātṛdīkṣā), the lineage (krama), and the supreme succession (paryāya).
O Karṇa, nothing else associated with the practice of the Yāmala should be performed by the initiate (samayin),
the spiritual son (putraka), the practitioner (sādhaka), and the teacher (ācārya).
The *citraka* should be a *pāraśava*, and the *śivadvija* belongs to the *putrakas*;
that which is joined with the *mātṛdīkṣā* is the *yośraka* of the four castes.
In the beginning, the Pāraśavas were indeed the constant worshippers of the Goddess;
among those fit for ritual action, the Pāraśavas were especially so, having been initiated.
The union of a Brāhmaṇa with a Śūdra maiden through the performance of mantras results in the birth of a Pāraśava; such a person is incapable of [performing] rites pertaining to caste and the like.
(89) Endowed with the sixteen [rites] and joined with all the purificatory ceremonies (saṃskāras),
the initiation of the Mother (mātṛdīkṣā) must be performed for one who is remembered as a corpse that has crossed over birth.
And for all others who are worthy, especially for everyone,
whatever rite is performed by one who has not been initiated shall be fruitless.
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform the worship of Pāraśava;
having especially performed the fire-oblation (homa) likewise equally in the four directions.
Raktā, Karālī, Caṇḍākṣī, and Mahocchiṣṭā are each [to be worshipped] individually;
and Khadira, Aśvattha, Bilva, and Vaṭa are likewise [to be placed] in the four directions.
One should offer one hundred and eight oblations for each [deity] individually; Brahmā indeed receives twenty-one.
These consist of fuel-sticks, clarified butter, sacrificial porridge, parched grain, mustard seeds, barley, and sesame seeds.
Mudga beans, bamboo shoots, śrī leaves, and plantain fruit—
each of these should be offered as oblations in the four directions in due order, accompanied by their respective mantras.
One should perform the fire-oblation with the nine-syllable mantra using fuel-wood as the substance,
according to the ritual procedure of the Kula-vidyā, and thereafter [proceed] with the acquisition of the village.
One should perform the festival in succession for seven days or three days;
or else, one may properly wander through the village for a single night.
At the conclusion of the circumambulation, one should especially perform the oblation according to the previously mentioned procedure;
having first performed the lotus-rite, the wise practitioner should cause the ceremonial bathing to take place.
Having caused the ceremonial bath to be performed according to the prescribed rules for bathing,
one should feed the Brahmins there in accordance with one's wealth.
One should cause food, drink, and other necessities to be given to the poor and the destitute;
however, when a defect arises in the fetus, these measures do not bring about a cure at all.
If one should commit an offense out of ignorance, there will be the calamity of death;
there will be famine, terrible strife, and drought.
This ritual has been proclaimed for the sake of removing defects related to pregnancy and age;
by performing it according to this procedure, all-pervading peace shall come to pass.
In the pure [state] of wealth and illusion, there shall be incomparable radiance;
let the region of the heart be grasped by means of the *praṇava* and indeed by the six-syllabled mantra.

The syllable *phaṭ* is at the region of the mouth, and likewise the syllable *huṃ* on the head; the two sides are marked with the letter *sa* together with its branches, and the syllable *hrīṃ* accompanied by the mantra is on the flanks.

By means of the sixteenfold seed-mantra of Śakti joined with *svāhā* and the *praṇava*, the practitioner of mantra attains prosperity; or else, he may take away the vital energy (*tejas*) residing within [the victim].
The wise practitioner should take the entire [substance], consecrated with the nine-syllable mantra;
having seen it well, he should cause it to be recited over with the root mantra.
Having caused [the disciple] to recite according to the ritual procedure, the wise practitioner should unite him with the root-vidyā;
then the mantra-knower should offer the remainder as a fire-oblation (homa) one hundred times with the nine-syllable mantra.
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī,
as well as Vārāhī, Indrāṇī, Cāmuṇḍī, and Vīrabhadra.
Gaṇeśa and likewise the guardians of the world (Lokapālas) are in that field,
as are the Piśācas, Pretas, Bhūtas, Kūṣmāṇḍas, and Guhyakas.
p.
91) The knower of mantras should cause the *gandharvas*, *kiṃnaras*, and *siddhas* to receive offerings from all [of them];
he should present the offering to them with the root mantra.
A wise man [should avoid] a crossroads, a triple-path, a pond, a field-ditch,
a rampart, a monastery, a cremation ground, or a shrine.
Everything remaining from the oblation belongs to him who is endowed with devotion and firm in his vows;
indeed, the wise man, being self-restrained, should offer red-colored food.
One should offer the bali-oblation according to the prescribed rite; the knower of mantras should cast away the red vessel outside, either beyond the village boundary or by placing it in a well.
Or afterwards, the wise man should sprinkle the sacrificial pit with dust;
there, he should feed twenty-one maidens.
Thus the ritual for the sacrificial animal (paśu) has been declared; now its characteristics are praised.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Sacrificial Animal," in the *Brahmayāmala-śatasahasra-saṃhitā*.
Henceforth, I shall explain according to the sequence of the Vedas:
the rites for pacification (śāntika), for nourishment (pauṣṭika), as well as those for malevolent magic (ābhicāraka) and killing (māraṇa).
Having performed the propitiatory rites in the proper sequence beginning with the Brahmins,
he described the successive emergence of the Mothers for the purpose of destroying the Asuras.
Having performed the rite of pacification for the Mothers, all beings will become well-disposed.
The sacrificial victim is said to be of three kinds: superior, middling, and inferior.
Having killed an elephant, a horse, or a human, one should designate it as the highest [offense];
a buffalo is indeed the middling, while a camel, a goat, or a pig is the lowest.
The *hariṇa* is the best, while the *kukkuṭa* is the lowest;
it has a white color on the forehead and is joined with eye-guggulu.
He whose flesh is like a mirror, who possesses beautiful eyes, who has a broad neck, large eyes, a vast body, and a great head—O Skanda! O you of great head!
If it lacks horns, there will be mental anguish; if it lacks eyes, there is loss of wealth;
if it lacks ears, there is indeed drought; and if it lacks feet, there is mud.
A toothless person faces death; one whose teeth are burnt by fire faces the destruction of their lineage; one with uneven teeth faces constant poverty; and one lacking teeth faces fear of the king.
We recognize that the embryo produced herein brings about the destruction of the afflictions of living beings;
therefore, being discerning, I shall again explain peace by means of application.
One should prepare a stone crystal [for the deity], which causes the outbreak of Mahāmārī;
one should perform its pacification, and thus peace is established once again.
One should perform an expiation, for it pacifies all faults;
[one should offer] a buffalo, complete in all its limbs, beautiful to behold, and very handsome.
Furthermore, one should bring there an animal as previously described, endowed with all auspicious marks,
of a beautiful color, auspicious, and possessing a pleasing appearance for its mount.
If it is black in color, there will be an abundance of food; if it has a smoky appearance, it shall be a vehicle. If there is a blue mark on the forehead, one will obtain cattle and happiness.
An eye resembling guggulu resin indicates the certain attainment of a son;
one with a short neck is long-lived, possesses auspicious marks, and brings happiness.
Thus, one who knows the rules and procedures should perform the ritual for the increase and prosperity of the Mothers;
having purified the sacrificial animal for five nights, he should also characterize it with the *caru* oblation.
In that regard, for the Mothers, a complete, pure, and unstained bath is prescribed;
it is said to be the best when performed separately for each of the five groups of eight.
Having specifically avoided those who are very young or very old,
one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) of the sacrificial animal on the sixth lunar day during the first part of the night.
In the center of the altar, one should fashion a square mandala;
with the mantra "huṃ phaṭ," it should be made eight-petaled with a pericarp.
Having likewise pervaded the middle with the *saptarohiṇī* mantra,
the best of men, endowed with devotion, should cut [it] with the root mantra.
One should perform the bali-rite at all festivals and similar occasions;
O Goddess, the procedure for the vehicle and the chariot is now being declared.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Ritual for Peace," in the *Brahmayāmala*, the compendium of one hundred thousand verses. 20.
(94) Hereafter I shall proclaim the supreme hoisting of the banner;
I shall describe the characteristics of the banner as superior, inferior, and middling.
It should be sixteen cubits in length and two and a half cubits in width;
at its base, it should be provided with a water-clock (ghaṭikā) and joined with the sound of small bells (kiṅkiṇī).
One should designate as the supreme banner of a Brāhmaṇa that which is white, equipped with a plantain tree on its side, and split in two at its top.
The trident, Śiva himself, the skull, as well as Kauśika,
the iron arrow, the axe, and likewise all manner of garments.
Marked at the beginning, middle, and end by these very [syllables],
it is produced from a white thread and endowed with manifold splendor.
Thus has the supreme banner been described; the middle one should be twelve [units] in length.
O Brahmin, one should have the middle banner made in due order, just as before.
The banner of a Kṣatriya is said to be five tālas in width, endowed with five colors, and provided with red thread.
The lowest [size] shall be ten cubits long and two cubits wide;
one should have it constructed there as before, adorned with various paintings.
That of a Vaiśya is endowed with a yellow color and measures eight cubits in length and two cubits in width.
For Śūdras, one should likewise have a painting made that is of the lowest quality, endowed with a single motif; as before, the cloth there should be black in color.
Cotton is prescribed for the Brāhmaṇa, while linen is for the Kṣatriya;
yellowish-brown is proclaimed for the Vaiśyas and Śūdras as the material for their banners.
The wise man should indeed draw Karālī there upon that cloth;
for this is the characteristic of the banners, categorized as superior, middling, and inferior.

One should perform the rite for the flagstaff (dhvajadaṇḍa) in its superior, middling, or inferior forms. The superior staff is said to be twice the height of the temple; this is declared to be the best.
Sandalwood, campaka, madhuka, and likewise panasa;
khadira, devadāru, vakula, and bilva as well.
The Aśoka tree is declared to be the best,
while the coconut tree is middling.
The lowest type of tree for a sage would be the *kramuka*; that which is fit for sacrifice should be known as made of bamboo; this is here called the measurement of the base.
These trees are praised when they possess the characteristics previously described,
and they should be one hundred cubits, or half of that, or likewise twenty or fifteen cubits in height.
Or one should employ a staff twelve cubits long;
know that it should be made of bamboo, for I am here spoken of by means of its root.
The circumference at the base should be sixteen finger-breadths, and it should be eight finger-breadths in the middle;
at its tip, however, it should be half of that—this is called the best staff.
For the middle [type], it should be half of that, according to the sequence;
and for the prāsāda, the base (mūla) should be eight aṅgulas, according to the sequence.
Having thus prepared the staff, the wise one should raise the banner;
or else, he may raise a wooden banner according to the prescribed sequence.
If one raises the banner in the morning, the kingdom shall attain victory;
at midday, there shall be prosperity for the kingdom; and in the evening, there is auspiciousness for men.
At midnight, it becomes Brahman; it shall bring about all prosperity.
It destroys the path of Agni and likewise [the path] of * * *.
It is the auspiciousness of all substances, the ornament of divine ornaments,
the destroyer of false gods, and the delight of the god-like sages.
Then the preceptor, having adorned him with all ornaments and being freed from the corpse,
should cause betel to be offered to everyone, especially to those [previously mentioned].
One should hoist the banner upon it according to the ritual prescribed in the scriptures;
having hoisted the banner of Brahman, one should proceed according to the rule.
When that [rain] falls near a banner, it is equal to the length of an outstretched arm;
in the region of Indra (the east) it shall be white in color, while in the region of Agni (the southeast) it shall be red in color.
In the south is that which arises from Kṛṣṇa, and in the southwest it is indeed smoke-colored;
in the west it has that same form, while in the northwest it is yellow in color.
In the case of Soma, it should have the luster of gold; in the case of Śaṅkara, it should have the hue of saffron.
Thus is described the long staff of one's own [deity], provided with a bamboo handle.
And likewise, the length of the three banners is stated;
or else, the measurement of the wooden staff is now being described.
Having performed this in brief, the wise one should cause the food offering (naivedya) to be presented;
the most excellent food offering consists of one *droṇa* of rice.
There should be half that amount of meat, combined with one *prastha* of ghee,
along with three banners and curds as a side dish.
Likewise, a coconut fruit combined with plantain fruit,
jaggery, sugar-candy, black gram, green gram, and root-fruits.
One should especially prepare *bṛhatī*, *kāravallī*, and *kūṣmāṇḍa*,
along with salt and black pepper, making them smooth with oil or fat.
There, one should cause the offering to be presented; this is remembered as the Kramapada rite.
It consists of milk-rice (pāyasa) mixed with honey, but devoid of curd.
The preceptor should cause a deity of his own lineage, a Vetāla with a sword in hand, to be presented;
likewise, the sacrificial offering (havis) should be offered to the deity of the banner (dhvajadeva).
One should cause betel-leaf to be offered therein and dedicate the deity of the banner;
thus indeed is the "excellent" rite proclaimed, especially with regard to the sacrificial oblation.
One should pierce half of that for the middle [line], and half of that again shall be the uneven [line].
Oṃ, we meditate upon the one with the sword in hand; we contemplate the deity of the banner.
May that Dhvaja inspire us;
may he inspire us from the position of the Paiśācīs, and from beyond that as well.
Having thus recited the mantra, one should perform everything right there:
first strike the drum, and afterwards raise the banner.
98) There, one should cause betel-leaf to be given to all according to their respective shares;
and upon the altar, one should place water-pots upon the rice-grains in due order.
Having prepared rice with eight *droṇas* of *śāli* rice in particular,
one should likewise thread five jewels and threads into the rice.
In the same manner, the wise one should indeed lay out the threads transversely;
within that, he should mark two squares at the heart and likewise in the four directions.
In the center, one should draw a nine-square lotus with eight petals and the syllable *ña* in its pericarp;
it should be scattered with barley and grains, and its width at the end should be four [units].
The wise one should adorn a lotus with a *āḍhaka* measure of sesame seeds,
and he should place the five precious gems into that pure water-pot.
It is wrapped with a thread, adorned with red mango sprouts,
provided with a pair of cloths, and accompanied by scented water.
Having done thus, O Brahmin, one should again cause the food offering (naivedya) to be presented;
and having brought the deity into the vicinity of the heart, one should offer the bali as previously described.
Having done thus in brief, one should perform the feeding of the maidens;
and one should feed sixteen maidens with milk-rice (pāyasa) using [sixteen] vessels.
On the northern side of the banner, however, is the pedestal of the Kṣetrapāla;
it may be circular, in a row of squares, triangular, or even square.
Alternatively, there may be a temple for the Goddess; the pedestal is said to be in the northeast.
Having raised it to one unit in width, the colored design should be of that same height.
Resembling a sapphire, with terrible fangs and a massive belly,
holding a staff in his hand, with beautiful hands and eyes, with hair standing erect and a terrifying face.
Having visualized [the deity] as having the luster of a cloud, one should offer the bali-oblation to the Kṣetrapāla;
the worship of the mantra should be performed with twenty-four syllables.
One should cast all the mantra-obstacles of the field as an offering to the Kṣetrapāla;
having first struck the drum, one should cast the offering there.
First, having made the ritual mark (aṅkura), one should then perform the ritual of the sword (asi-vāsana);
after that, having raised the banner (dhvaja), one should finally strike the drum (bherī).
At the end of that, one should perform the Śrī-bali; at the end of that, likewise the aṅkura;
at the end of that, the sacrifice and worship; and at the end of that, likewise the Śrī-bali.
At the conclusion of that, a festival is prescribed; at its conclusion, perform the ritual bathing, and at its conclusion, the worship of the Guru according to the rite seen in the scriptures.
I shall describe the offering to the Kṣetrapāla according to the prescribed procedure;
it should be cooked with one hundred prasthas, or half of that, according to specific requirements.
It is cooked with goat meat, combined with powdered rice-flakes,
and mixed with pieces of jaggery and pieces of sugarcane.
Combined with plantain fruit and accompanied by honey and clarified butter,
the wise man should likewise offer this oblation while all musical instruments are played.
Therefore, with every effort, one should offer the bali-oblation on the day of Mars;
specifically, on the day preceding that day.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Ritual for Hoisting the Banner," in the *Vīravidhāna* section of the *Brahmāyāmala*.
100) Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the bali offering for the day of Mars; listen!
It removes all sins for the king and increases all prosperity.
It is for the welfare of the Brahmins, the destruction of great pestilence,
the victory of kings and kingdoms, and the increase of sons and grandsons.
It destroys domestic fevers, eliminates malevolent spirits,
brings about great peace, and increases abundant rainfall.
The Rājasena [yantra] is for the sake of happiness, for the increase of elephants, horses, and men,
for freedom from fear of thieves and enemies, and for increasing the joy of one's mothers.
Therefore, with every effort, one should offer the *bali* for the family-day (*kulavāra*).
On the day preceding that [specific] day, one should bind the thread at night.
When the preparation is perfected with eight *droṇas*, one should draw a lotus there;
having performed it according to this procedure, one should sprinkle it while reciting the root mantra.
Having placed a water-pot in the center of that [mandala], excluding the black circle,
one should wrap it with three threads and fill it well with scented water.
The preceptor should place Ekavīrī, endowed with the five jewels and adorned with two garments, into the jar while reciting the root mantra.
One should offer incense, flowers, a lamp, water for honor (arghya), and sacrificial porridge (caru);
having worshipped the "unaging red" [deity], one should bind the left hand.
At the clear and pure dawn,
one should begin the sprinkling with water after having diligently performed double the worship according to the rites prescribed in the scriptures.
Having thus performed the ritual procedure with cooked rice, parched grain, fruits, and so forth,
the preceptor should offer oblations there for one day with the root mantra.
Having placed [the offerings] before the Goddess, the preceptor should perform the worship of the Mothers in either a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila),
using the mantra of the Mothers.
A fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed there; one should offer oblations in that place in the proper sequence:
blood, meat, ghee, mustard seeds, and likewise sesame seeds.
One should offer oblations eight times each, consisting of parched grain, cakes, and other such items;
one should place the Bhūtapīṭha in the center and cause the *ajasapta* to fall.
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of both the manifest (sakala) and the unmanifest (niṣkala), one should offer that blood,
which is joined with the three sweets and mixed with wine.
Having joined it with the middle meat, one should place it upon the girdle;
having performed it according to this procedure, the supreme preceptor should join it.
A trident, a banner, an axe, a food-liṅga, and the instrument of ritual action;
likewise a skull, a hand-drum, and a jewel-studded tiger-skin.
Having extracted these [mantras] and placed them within one initiated as a supreme Śaiva,
one should indeed cause an offering to be made while holding a razor in hand.
Accompanied by various large drums, provided with various musical instruments,
joined with the sound of hand-drums (ḍamaruka), and endowed with everything [else].
Endowed with devotion to the Mother and united with Māheśvarī,
there are the Samayin, the Sādhaka, as well as the Putraka and the Ācārya.
With the hand resting on a knife, one should quickly offer a bali-oblation on a Tuesday at midday in a beautiful place where there is a gathering.
Whether in a village or a city, or even in a hamlet or a small settlement;
at a crossroads, a triple junction, a threshing floor, or likewise upon an anthill.
One should cause the bali offering to be given everywhere, at crossroads and in cremation grounds;
however, during the time of the bali procession, people must not step over it.
Having performed the leap over the trident, one shall attain liberation;
this applies even when such a leap occurs there in the case of women and Brahmins.
One should act without hesitation, and having performed the *bali* offering, one should wander about.
If a Vaiśya or a Kṣatriya transgresses, one should cause a cutting of flesh to be made.
This applies equally to dogs, cats, buffaloes, donkeys, and camels as well.
O knower of mantras, one should cause even the bound souls (paśus) to be slain by means of the root mantra.
Thus, O Brahmin, one should offer the bali; hear now the definitive conclusion of the scripture.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Offering on Tuesday," in the *Brahmayāmala*, the compendium of one hundred thousand verses.
O Lotus-seated One, listen as I describe the festival for a single day:
having constructed a pavilion as before, complete with arches and banners.
The Vaidika [mandala] is square, with forty units (kulās) in sequence;
outside of that, one should likewise construct the door and the sugarcane stalks.
The measurements should be one *ratni* on all four sides and square;
the dark fortnight is recommended, specifically the fourteenth day of the month of Aṅgāraka.
On the day of Aṅgāraka (Mars), there is an excellent festival in Rohiṇī;
likewise, on the day of Aṅgāraka, there is [a festival] in Puṣya, which belongs to Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
One should perform the monthly rite and present the offering of charcoal;
one should worship the Goddess in the forenoon and present the *kūrca* grass-bundle as an offering.
One should perform the pacifying oblation (śāntihoma) together with the goddess and the fire according to the prescribed rules;
first, one should offer blood-water as the sacrificial offering (bali) during the midday bali-rite.
And minced meat, blood, parched grain, and equal measures [of other substances],
as well as many cakes and bundles of kusha grass.
One should worship the sacrificial offerings and the weapons according to the mantras,
accompanied by incense and lamps, with a canopy adorned with cloth.
It was adorned with the Madhudhvaja, the Sahañca, the Pāśa, and likewise the Majjaka; it was further embellished by a sword, a quiver, a bow, a scimitar, and a kṛccha weapon.

One should perform the offering of oblations (bali-rakṣā); the master of the ritual, accompanied by his attendants, should lead [the offerings] there, holding the vessel for the oblation and his weapon, remaining silent and devoted to his vow.
A celibate student, an ascetic, and a pure Brahmin shall sit together;
having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the Mātṛkā-mantra, [the site] is made beautiful.
One should fashion the seven seals and the archways according to their conventional designations;
the wise practitioner should offer the bali-oblation to the guardians of the field and install them there.
Having wandered around the *ālaya*, they then proceed gradually,
circumambulating either a village, a city, or a town.
First, one should offer a bali-oblation to Brahmadevī at the station of Brahmā;
then, one should perform bali-offerings all around, from Indra up to Īśāna.
Or else, wearing the attire of the Goddess and holding her mudrā after the offering of the bali,
one should first prepare a square maṇḍala in the southeast, shaped like a womb (yonimākṛti).
One should know that in the south there is a half-moon, in the southwest a triangle,
in the west a circle, and in the northwest a hexagon.
A wise person should cause a mandala to be made, measuring one cubit in size, with an eight-petaled lotus in the north and an eight-cornered figure in the northeast.
As well as step-wells, wells, ponds, and likewise city gates.
In a temple, in an assembly hall, in a pavilion, or in a monastery; in the midst of a forest, in a dwelling place, or at a banyan tree, a plakṣa tree, or a cremation ground.
At the four gates of the city, at a single tree, and at a temple of Śiva,
one who knows the mantras should especially offer an oblation under his own name.
Having repeatedly honored [the deity] with the binding of mudrās and prostrations,
one should afterwards present the bali offering and recollect the bali mantra.
Having performed the journey-rite (yātrā) and the fire-oblation (homa), especially that pertaining to Pāraśava,
one should recite the fourfold [mantra] and then recite the Heart-mantra of Cāmuṇḍā.
At that time, at midnight, the supreme worship of the Goddess is performed;
it consists of a great, eightfold sound following the offering of the *bali*.
Having worshipped, in due order, with the name-mantra of the Moon, which brings forth the qualities of the two nines...
The wise man should worship those seated there with *arghya*, *pādya*, and *ācamanīya*, ending with the *arghya*; he should then deposit the *bali* offerings right there.
Having especially worshipped all those ending with the cremation ground, there should be an offering of oblations at night; then one should begin their ritual bathing.
One should offer a special oblation and, having sacrificed an animal, present it;
the wise man should honor the preceptor with garments, ornaments, and decorations.
Thus should the wise man perform this rite, which destroys all suffering and yields the merit of visiting all sacred fords, equal to the fruit of giving away a thousand cows.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Single-Day Festival," in the *Brahmayāmala*, the compendium of one hundred thousand verses. 23.
Having thus performed the great festival, the wise one should cause the *vabhratha* rite to be performed;
specifically at the full commencement and especially when it is complete in the presence of the Goddess.
The wise man should construct a square pavilion measuring ten cubits using cow dung; he should establish the sprouts there and place śāli rice grains within it.
One should place the mortar there, and one should place it there with its roots;
one should worship the two deities there in the middle of the mortar and pestle.
One should place the Yoginī there and offer incense, flowers, and so forth;
having invoked the Goddess, one should perform the rite of completion in the eastern direction.
One should scatter the powder upon the twice-born; otherwise, one incurs fault.
The wise man should place that powder there while reciting the root mantra.
The retinue should bathe [the image], followed by anointing with oil;
they should also worship the patron (yajamāna) or [place the offerings] upon the heads of all.
Having thoroughly wandered through the village, the wise man should perform his ritual bath in a river;
or, having gone toward a blameless direction, he may do so at a lake.
Then, according to the procedure for the casting of the bath, one should perform the river-bath with eight jars in succession,
and afterwards, having removed the protective thread.
All those who do not live by improper means may perform their bath according to their desire;
after bathing, one who is self-controlled should properly give gifts according to his capacity.
Returning again to the *ālaya*, one should perform the flower sacrifice;
with flowers of five colors, one should draw the previously mentioned maṇḍala.
One should properly worship the Mothers in the maṇḍala with the root-mantra on a beautiful morning, adorned with all ornaments.
The wise man should offer the vessel-oblation in a *kutapa* cloth, and the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) for all castes in a vessel of gold, silver, copper, or bell-metal.
Whether by hundreds of thousands (*niyuta*), or tens of thousands (*ayuta*), or likewise five thousand;
or by thousands, or half a thousand, or again half of that half, or half of that half.
And likewise, having bathed him, one should adorn him with red garments,
anoint him with red perfumes, and [offer] the supreme noose and goad.
A skull-topped staff, a conch, a discus, and likewise a mace in the hands;
a thunderbolt, a spear, a banner, a lotus, and likewise a svastika.
With all these [ingredients], one should slowly perform a circumambulation of the village or even the city, which is surrounded by maidens according to their respective positions.
This food, consisting of kṛsarā and cakes,
as well as red rice accompanied by flowers, should be consecrated with the nine-syllable mantra.
One should cause the bali offering, conjoined with each respective mantra, to be given everywhere;
having held it upon one's head, one should slowly perform circumambulation.
Having performed [the preliminary rites] according to the rule, one should enter immediately after the Goddess;
having performed a special bath, one should offer incense, lamps, and oblations.
Likewise, one who is a *pāraśava* by birth should offer [the oblation] with the *pṛthu-mantra*.
There are four [types]: *bhraṃśa*, *bhāra*, *tila*, and *śālipriyaṅgu*.
Having worshipped the beautiful [deity] there, one should offer everything;
then, having taken that handful, the wise practitioner should perform the fire-oblation (homa).
The practitioner should likewise offer one hundred and eight oblations of sacrificial fuel (*samidh*) with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*).
Then, by means of the rite of oblation, one should offer sesame, śāli rice, and priyaṅgu;
let that [oblation] reach me, and there will be total pacification.
Furthermore, one should offer the remainder of the oblation as a *bali* in the ten directions;
the remaining portion should be respectfully given as a *bali* to the *kṣetrapāla*.
One should first feed the maiden, and at the conclusion of the sacrifice, feed the twice-born;
afterwards, one should honor the preceptor with garments, gold, and rings.
One should likewise worship the attendants and followers everywhere;
thus is described the *tālabali*, which destroys all diseases.
It brings abundance of food, prosperity, and the increase of sons and grandsons.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Ritual of the Bali Offering," in the *Brahmayāmala*, the compendium of one hundred thousand verses.
The Lord said:
In a pleasant spot at the edge of the village, one should afterwards perform the ritual bathing;
having first performed the powder-bath, likewise perform the curd-bath.
One should wrap the mortar and pestle, which are combined with all kinds of perfumes and mixed with colored powders, in a pair of cloths.
The preceptor should pulverize [the obstacles] with the root mantra for those disciples who possess sons;
there, he should worship the Ācārya, who is adorned with the very sprout.
Having taken all the powder, one should perform the ablution with the root-mantra;
then, having bathed separately with the Īśī-mantra, one should subsequently worship Mātrā.
One should worship the attendant piśācas, the seats of yoga (yogapīṭhas), and the yoginīs; thereafter, one should worship the preceptor and then the patron.
The lineage descendants and the sons [should perform the rites] for all, or specifically for the head;
thereafter, having bathed in a river, one should proceed toward the auspicious direction while avoiding those who speak ill.
A pond should be constructed according to the great [treatises];
having approached a reservoir of water, prepare rice with sand.
Having placed jars filled with all kinds of food, one should thereafter perform the ritual bathing (snāna),
provided with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata).
One should release the protection cord with the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
Then, all those people, having bathed with focused attention, [should proceed].

Having given gifts according to one's ability— be they cattle, land, gold, or anything else— at a sacred gift-bestowing site or a place of pilgrimage, one shall attain the heavenly world as the fruit of that giving.
Returning again to the ālaya, one should begin the ritual bathing;
having adorned it with five colors, one should place a lotus with eight petals.
Then one should worship the pericarp, complete with filaments, with perfumes and other offerings;
in its center, one should place the Śaiva [icon] and offer perfumes, flowers, and food.
One should perform the ceremonial bathing (snapana) of the Śaiva [deity] according to the ritual procedure prescribed in the scriptures,
having prepared a square mandala measuring ten cubits.
The wise man, having prepared rice from śāli grains using one droṇa,
or half of that, or even half of that again, or alternatively using five droṇas;
One should take half of that for the mandala and draw a lotus in the center;
or [the symbols] may be a thousand, or half of that, or even half of that again.
Alternatively, it is prescribed that there be one hundred and eight or eighty-five earthen jars,
excluding the kalaśa and the maṇḍala.
Having prepared them, washed them until they were pure, and fumigated them with guggulu resin;
[the vessels] should be provided with cords, bound with threads, equipped with strainers, and furnished with lids.
Having made the pavilion beautiful, adorned with canopies and banners,
encircled by garlands of *darbha* grass, and well-decorated with wreaths of flowers.
It is joined with six sets of eight [articles], provided with fruits and sprouts,
equipped with chowries and mirrors, and accompanied by bells and incense.
Among the twenty-five jars, the principal one is proclaimed;
[the others contain] water for the feet, water for sipping, the arghya offering, the five products of the cow, and water with sesame seeds.
Milk, curd, and ghee, as well as honey and molasses;
water with flowers, water with fruits, scented water, and water with *kuśa* grass.
Water purified with saffron, water from a metal vessel, water from three types of grass,
water for pacification (śāntyudaka), water from a forest spring, and likewise water for pacification (śāntyudaka).
Then, in sequence, there are the juice of sugarcane with pleasant speech, iron-water,
and the water of the eight jewels— these twenty-five [substances].

Having offered water for the feet and other items with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, one should place all nine [deities] starting from Indra up to Īśāna; they should be arranged by circumambulation in a clockwise direction.
p. 111) One should perform the consecration (abhiṣeka), accompanied by the twenty-five *kalās* and the primary pitchers,
using well-consecrated pure water.
Having worshipped all [the deities] repeatedly with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings,
one should separately place the water-pots and encircle them with thread alone.
The place for the water for the feet (*pādya*) is prescribed by means of the nine-syllable mantra;
having sipped water with the nine-syllable mantra, the wise one should offer the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*).
Having recited the mantra in the heart, one should perform the ritual bath with the *arghya* water;
O knower of mantras, the wise practitioner should then apply the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) with the root mantra.
Then, the knower of mantras should offer water with sesame seeds using the *śikhā* mantra;
the preceptor should then perform the rite with consecrated milk according to the proper sequence.
Having recited the knowledge-mantra (vidyāmantra), the ritual bath for the observance (vratasnāna) is prescribed.
The wise one, with the nine-syllable mantra, should contemplate the remainder of everything in due order;
and with the weapon-mantra, he should contemplate himself and the individual water-pots separately.
The preceptor, wearing red garments, having bathed with purity and subdued his senses, [should be present];
there the Goddess, her self well-guarded, is endowed with all auspicious marks.

One who is devoid of the *nāga* [constellation] is deaf; one born under the *śaṭha* [constellation] is likewise so; one born under *kūra* is cruel; one with limbs reddened by *nāga* is afflicted by disease; and those under *utma* and *artha* are oppressed by ritual constraints.
O Śiva, O twice-born one, you who know the nectar of all limbs, you who possess the six paths and are wise, endowed with those characteristics; [by you]—
Having bathed [the deity] according to the prescribed rite, one should offer *caru* (sacrificial porridge), excluding the seventh [color],
in the colors red, yellow, black, turmeric-yellow, dark-green, and so forth.
Milk-rice, rice-and-pulse, and the seven oblations are thus proclaimed; among the sacrificial animals for offerings, the white goat is praised.
Having offered [the oblation] according to the prescribed rite, perform the bali-offering at the five locations—
either one thousand, or one hundred, or fifty, or twenty-five [times].
It should be borne upon the head of a maiden, adorned with fragrant flowers,
and provided with variegated banners, flags, conchs, and drums.
One should perform a circumambulation of either a village or a city;
having approached a temple, one should simultaneously offer the sacrificial oblation (bali).
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Ritual of Bathing," in the *Brahmayāmala*, the compendium of one hundred thousand verses. 25.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the supreme rite of the maṇḍala,
which fulfills all desires and brings benefit to all the worlds.
The *mātṛśānti*, the *yoga*, and the *balikarma* should be written [on a cloth];
the best [size] is nine cubits, eight cubits, or seven cubits.
The mandala measuring five cubits and four cubits is likewise the medium one;
the smallest mandala should be three, two, or one cubit in size.
The Brahmin’s maṇḍala is the best, that of the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya is middling, and the Śūdra’s maṇḍala is the lowest; for all of them, it is joined with a maṇḍala.
At those joints which belong to the deities, the teacher should cross over;
[he should proceed] from the east toward the northern end as previously described, and by way of the south.
In the west, however, it should have its tip pointing north; in the north, its tip should point east;
and likewise, the east, south, west, and north [should be arranged accordingly].
One should construct four gates in the four directions and in the center;
[one should assign] Rakṣohaṇa and Phala as the guardians of the eastern gate.
In the southeast is the goddess Jvālinī; in the southwest is Viṣukarṇinī;
in the northwest is the goddess Ghātakī; and likewise, in the northeast is Īśvarī.
Having drawn the outer enclosure, the seventh [enclosure] is increased;
[the guardians are] Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, and likewise Varuṇa.
Vāyu, Soma, and Īśāna are the eight deities;
one should place Indra and Agni between the two doors, and the Aśvins in due order.
One should designate the station of the Pitṛs between the regions of Agni and Yama;
and one should likewise place the Yakṣas between the regions of Yama and Nairṛta.
One should place Nirṛti between Varuṇa and the Rākṣasas;
the station for the Ṛṣis is ordained between Varuṇa and Vāyu.
One should arrange eight serpents between Vāyu and Soma;
one should place the eleven Rudras between Soma and Kaiśāna.
Between Indra and Īśāna is Soma; there the deity presides.
This eighth, supreme station of the deities, they traverse.
Vimalī, Bhadrī, Kālakaṇṭhī, Sukaṇṭhinī,
Lambinī, Uttamī, Vikṛti, and Śuddhamohinī.
Hāṭakī is most terrible, deformed, and possessing high-set fangs;
she is playful, has misshapen eyes, and is four-armed, bearing a conch and a discus.
The fifth [group] revolves clockwise starting from the east:
Caṇḍā, Caṇḍamukhī, Ugrī, and Siṃhanādamahāravī.
Dvākuṭī and Bhīmarūpī, Ākāśī and Mandabuddhinī, Lakṣmī and Satyavādī, and likewise Krodhinī.
The Manavī, Mādhavī, and Rudrī revolve as the fourth;
likewise the Cakrī, Hutāśī, Yāmyānī, and Bhūtavāruṇī.
Vāyavī, Kauberī, Śaṅkarī holding a trident in her hand,
Kaṭvāṅgī, Candradhārī, Caṇḍadhārī, and Cakāriṇī.
The three-eyed one, the enjoyer of heroes, and likewise the one whose form is the Vedas;
these exist as the second [set], beginning with Indra and the others in their proper order.
One should worship [the deities] beginning with Brāhmī and ending with Vīravighna, starting from Indra and proceeding to Īśāna;
and in the center, one should install Yogeśvarī.
Budha, Kālī, Karālī, and Virālī—
these fourteen are indeed his forms within the mandala.
Otherwise, one should construct the mandala to its western side,
measuring four cubits in extent and endowed with the proper characteristics.
Having placed a trident in the center of that [space], with a skull-bowl on its side,
one should place the dancing ground outside of that, and the *kelaka* in the four directions.
The wise one should perform dance, song, instrumental music, and the display of mudrās;
he should employ the mudrā of the directions, starting from Indra in the east, up to Īśāna in the northeast.
Having placed the terrible [form] in the eastern direction, one should go to the abode of Śiva;
having placed the fierce, terrible, and fear-inspiring [form] in the southern direction.
Having placed [the hand] in the western direction, one should join the fingers in a weeping gesture;
having placed it in the northern direction, one should likewise join it with the face turned toward the sun.
Making a terrible sound like the fierce howling of jackals and uttering the cry of a female jackal,
he saw a full water-pot and a lotus among the *daṇḍaka* trees.
Having paid homage to and worshipped the door-keepers in their proper order,
the wise one should perform the ritual installation and worship with the mantra beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*.
Having worshipped that which stands in the middle of the bond of one's own name, the knower of his own mantra [should perform] the vajra, the bell, the casting down, and the fire-enclosure.
Having raised the mountain and the trident with four bindings by means of the Śūlamudrā,
one should then perform a prostration and likewise worship at the base of the trident.
One should display the bell, the razor, the sword, and so forth, ending with the mace;
in the ritual action, one should employ the mantra, the mudrā, and the offering of bali.
If a weapon falls while being hurled by a strong man, one should make it fall again;
however, if it has slipped from the hand, it must undergo the consecration ritual once more.
The preceptor should cause the offering of the *bali* to be performed from its commencement until its conclusion; should the householder practitioner,
through negligence or lack of attention, spill blood, [he must perform atonement].
Having offered the bali-oblation to the directions, let the Bhairavas come;
having carried out the command and what is beneficial, let the one who commits violence indeed destroy [the obstacle].
Alternatively, having performed non-violence, the fire oblation, and the worship of the eight directions,
and subsequently honored the *caru* offering, one should perform the expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Ritual of the Maṇḍala," in the *Brahmayāmala*, the compendium of one hundred thousand verses.
Hereafter, I shall explain the ritual of the musical instruments;
then, having performed the circumambulation while sounding the *saṃkalasa* drums, [one should proceed].
Relying on the second [water], one should begin the third with the *naṭa*;
the fourth is the *pañcanāṭya*, and the fifth is the *karmanāṭyaka*.
Ālīṭa is the third, and Pratyālīṭa is the fourth;
the fifth is Śayana; these are known as the five types of dance (pañcanāṭya).
Having likewise performed the eight-fold binding, the thumbs should be contracted;
the little fingers and the index fingers joined constitute the armor mudrā (kavacamudrā).
In the eastern direction is the weapon; in the eastern direction is the deity.
In the eastern direction, tell me of the son of the Mother.
Having made the deity of the east [the first], these [deities] shall be the deities;
one should cause the lineage of the Brāhmaṇa to prosper and offer water with the hollowed palms (añjali).
Tell me the mantra of the southern direction, the deity of the southern direction;
tell me, O Mother, [the mantra] of my son in the southern direction.
Whatever belongs to the southern direction, Yama indeed shall be the deity;
for the increase of the Kṣatriya family, one should offer water with cupped hands.
The mantra of the western direction and the deity of the western direction—
speak of the western direction, speak to me, O son of the Mother!
In the west, the deity Varuṇa is proclaimed there as the presiding divinity;
for the increase of the Vaiśya lineage, one should offer water with the hollowed palms (añjali).
The mantra of the northern direction,
the deity of the northern direction— speak it for me, O Mother, speak it to me, O Son!
In the north, however, that same deity is Kubera;
as with the Śūdra, one should take water for the sake of increasing the family with the añjali gesture.
Tell me the mantra for the single direction, the deity of the upward direction,
and speak to me of the son of the Mother in the half-direction.
O all-gods, may the deities in every direction be composed;
for the sake of increasing the lineage of the Mothers, one should take water in the hollowed palms.
Tell me the mantra of the lower direction and the deity of the lower direction;
tell me, O Mother, [the deity] of the lower direction, my little son.
p.
118) Let the deities of the single upward direction be concentrated upon all the gods;
for the sake of increasing the lineage of the Mothers, one should take water with the hollowed palms (añjali).
Tell me the mantra of the downward direction and the deity in the downward direction;
tell me, O son of my mother, who resides in the downward direction.
One should offer with cupped palms (añjali) the water for the deities below, as well as Viṣṇu as the deity, the Earth, all the Gaṇas, and the Waters.
Having constructed a square pavilion adorned with four doors,
one should place Vidyādhara in the east and likewise Garuḍa in the south.
In the west, the mandala itself is described; in the north, it should be tawny.
Thus, having fixed the face upon the mudrā, one should employ the sound of the bell.
Likewise, the preceptor, holding a sword-hilt and encircled by a sword,
performs a dance and presents it toward the eastern direction.
The mudrās of the directions, the dance of the directions, established by the four masters;
likewise, the ālīḍha posture and the lotus mudrā.
The right hand should be placed on the crest-lock (śikhā) and so forth, while the left foot is held with ghee;
the right foot is joined with the foot [of the deity], and the left hand is held with ghee.
Yakṣa and Gaṇaphaṇa are the two gatekeepers in the east;
Sumukha and Kāladaṇḍa are the two gatekeepers in the south.
Sakala and Kumbhakarṇa were the guardians of the northern gate;
Airāvata and Kuśa likewise held the bow and the arrow.
The vajra, the mūdrara, and likewise the pāśa—
these are declared to be the mudrās in the eastern direction, in their proper sequence.
Incense, the altar, the mudrā, and the fire-pit shall be at the heart;
with the mudrā, one should perform the prostration and the *praṇava* in the south-eastern direction.
Likewise, Kūpodaṇḍa, Pāśa, Śārvalīnaraka,
Vetālī, and Mahiṣa are in the southern direction with the mudrā of Thāmpā.
One should know the mudrās for the weapons of the Southwestern direction: the vāsa, the bhalam, the bhindi-pāla, the mudgara, the tomara, and also the kunta.
He saw a celestial chariot with its bells sounding, a lotus,
a full water-pot, and a lotus flower making a clockwise circumambulation upon the ground.
Merely by touching the heart, it is proclaimed as the Earth Mudrā;
likewise [are formed] the Moon, the Sun, the planets, the lunar mansions, and the stars.
And Brahmā and the seven ṛṣis are in the upward direction with their respective mudrās;
he wears a crown of matted hair, has three eyes, and is adorned with serpents.
The trident, the axe, the shield, and the skull-topped staff shall be the eighth;
O Vīreśa, these along with the *āgama-mudrā* are the means for accomplishing all desires and goals.
A rosary, a lotus, a water-pot, and likewise kuśa grass;
a staff, a black antelope skin, and a sacred thread with a swan-shaped loop.
Brahmāṇī and Aṅgamudrā accomplish all ritual purposes;
[the weapons are] the trident, the axe, the deer, and likewise the serpent and the bull.
An elephant hide, matted locks, and likewise a tiger skin,
as well as Vāmeśī and the Aṅga-mudrā, accomplish the purpose of all ritual actions.
The vajra, the śakti, and the bell, as well as the spear and the cock;
both types of sacred thread, and the sacrificial ladle and the pestle.
Kaumārī, the Aṅga-mudrā, which accomplishes all desires and purposes;
the lotus, the nine-fold garland, and Garuḍa shall be the eighth.
The Vaiṣṇavī Aṅgamudrā indeed accomplishes all desires and purposes;
likewise, one should [visualize] the fangs, the staff, the plow, Vārāhī, and the buffalo.
The sword, the discus, the mace, Vārāhī, and the finger-ring;
likewise the thunderbolt, the mace, the spear, the bow, and the iron arrow.
The *tomara*, the *bhiṇṭapāla*, and the *valaya* shall be the eighth;
and the *indrāṇī* is the *aṅgamudrā*, which accomplishes all desired aims.
A trident, a sword, a bow, an arrow, and a shield;
likewise a katvāṅga, a skull, a bell, and a hand-drum (ḍamaruka).
Cāmuṇḍī is indeed the Cāṅga-mudrā, which accomplishes all desires and purposes;
[one should meditate on] Gajānana, who has an elephant's trunk, elephant tusks, and a large belly.
The rosary, the mouthful of food, the tuft of hair, and the young disciple,
as well as Gaṇeśa, the limbs, and the mudrā— these accomplish all desired aims.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Rule for the Characteristics of Mudrās," in the *Brahmayāmala*, the compendium of one hundred thousand verses.
(121) Having attained Śiva, the Great Lord is indeed one and the same in all his limbs; for it is said that Śiva-nature is everything, and everything is indeed a union.
Henceforth, O Brahmā, I shall proclaim the characteristics of the various types; I will explain them according to the prescribed rule, exactly as they are, in their proper sequence.
The inner sanctum is called the *ālaya*, and the *daṇḍa* is said to be the temple structure itself.
Having constructed the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) as half the length of the *daṇḍa*, the inner *hāraka* (necklace-like molding) should extend the full length of the *daṇḍa*.
The middle chamber shall be two *daṇḍas* wide, while the middle wall shall be four *daṇḍas*;
the great boundary wall shall likewise be seven *daṇḍas*.
One should cause it to be constructed very firmly, either with stones or even with bricks, in successive stages; it may then be one cubit, two cubits, or three cubits in height.
The end of the feet, the end of the elevated portion, and the end of the neck—these three are elongated;
thus, in that very sequence, the enclosure wall is completely filled.
Having thus performed the work of whitewashing, one should prepare a well-adorned comfortable seat,
as well as the path, the enclosure wall, and the pavilion, using lime-paste.
The enclosure wall may be derived from the mother [lineage] or otherwise; the enclosure wall is traditionally said to be of three kinds:
entirely sacred, entirely variegated and prosperous, or even half-variegated.
One should also have groups of *bhūtas* and *pretas*, as well as forms of *piśācas* and *vetālas*,
fashioned there according to the extent of one's available wealth.
The sides are equal to the back, while the front is likewise double;
this is declared for the *antarhāra* [type of pavilion], and the temple (*cālaya*) is likewise in the *antarhāra*.
The eight [shrines] for the retinue should have their ālayas equal to that [of the main deity];
the door and the gate-tower (gopura) should be equal in measure to the temple of the Goddess.
One should designate the purpose for the *ālaya* or for the main object;
however, a square pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) should be constructed in front of the steps of the gateway.
A pavilion (maṇḍapa) should be constructed, or likewise a peaked roof (kūṭa);
the pedestal (pīṭha) should be situated within the inner enclosure, and one should worship the pedestal in the northeast (aindra).
Then, at midday, one should construct the stable for the vehicle in front;
the abode for the other attendants should be in the middle.
To the east of the Ālaya, however, is the Ādityālaya itself;
in the south-east is the forest site, and likewise the sequence of the Pacanālaya.
In the south, or in the Mātṛgṛha (temple of the Mothers), or likewise on the back or the side;
in the southwest is the place for the herd of cattle and the pavilion for the storage of grain.
In the west is the location for Lakṣmī and likewise the kitchen;
in the south is the temple of the Mothers, as well as [the quarters] at the back and the sides;
the temple of Skanda is in the northwest, while the treasury is in the north.
And likewise, there should be a temple of Durgā, as well as a dwelling for serpents.
In the northeast is the water-place; the Bhairava-sthāna of the Noble One is likewise in front, as are the Bhūta-pīṭha and the Dhvaja-pīṭha.
The Paśupīṭha, the Surāpīṭha, and the Piśācapīṭha are on the exterior;
one should perform them according to the prescribed rule, just as Śiva himself has declared.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Rule for the Characteristics of the Enclosure Wall," in the *Brahmayāmala-śatasahasra-saṃhitā*. (p. 123)

Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the sequence of rites for the deities of the locations:
at a crossroads, at a triple-path, and likewise at a corner for Kapardin.

Having worshipped in due order according to the prescribed ritual with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings,
one should perform a great festival at night to the sounding of conchs, kettledrums, and other instruments.
Having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, one should likewise bind the thread;
at the beginning of all rites, the declaration of an auspicious day must be performed for all activities.
The fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed at night, and the installation (sthāpana) should be carried out at dawn;
on an auspicious day and at a favorable moment (sumuhūrta), one should cause the child to enter the place of residence.
O Kālamantha, knower of the ritual procedures, as long as the collection of palaces stands,
so long shall [the deity] remain in Baligrāma for twenty-one and twelve [years] respectively.
One should establish [the practice] by means of the *āsthāpana* procedure with the *hṛdaya* mantra;
for the *āsthāpana* is, in its very essence, the foundation of all stabilizing rites (*sthāpanā*).
The wise one should place the vases upon the image with the nine-syllable mantra;
he should then sprinkle everything with the water from the vase using the heart-mantra.
The most excellent preceptor should sprinkle with water the pedestal, the womb, the wall, the temple, or the pavilion, as well as all the attendant deities.
Having slain an animal right there, one should, being composed, offer its blood to the Goddess of the Gods with the Heart mantra, whether three or even just one.
There, one should cause the offerings to be presented with garments and ornaments as well;
afterwards, one should feed the Brahmins and feed seven young maidens.
Then, all the castes [should offer] in order;
therefore, one equipped with weapons should present the *bhūtabali* in the village, which is the dwelling of men.
One should offer the bali-oblation mixed with parched grain flour everywhere;
having offered the bali with the heart-mantra, the wise one [should likewise offer it] at the bali-pīṭha.
One should honor all the teachers with garments, gold, and rings,
as well as the materials required for the sacrifice, including clothing and ornaments.
"But the teacher [bestows] various diseases according to the substance [offered].

Half of that [measure] is rice, half of that is sesame,

Palāśa, khadira, aśvattha, plakṣa, and nyagrodha;

It was filled with dancing and instrumental music, endowed with various sounds,

Accompanied by the sound of the Vedas,

as well as within the temple and its surrounding precincts, both externally and internally.
The wise one should sprinkle everything as previously described and perform the placement of the root-mantra;
then, he should invoke the Goddess, who is endowed with all auspicious characteristics.
She has eight arms and three eyes, is adorned with serpent ornaments,
wears a serpent as a sacred thread, and has her head decorated with a garland of snakes.
One should install the Goddess Maheśvarī, the source of the universe and the sustainer of all during dissolution,
within the image, especially on a Tuesday.

From that time forward, the most wealthy person should worship there with diligence; and at that very moment, the consecration should be performed by the preceptor and those who recite auspicious blessings.
With various ornaments and materials, such as cattle, land, gold, and so forth.

Henceforth, O Brahmin, listen with a concentrated mind as I shall proclaim the sequence of rules for the conduct of the sacred fields (kṣetra) and the successive order of the castes (varṇa).
Service to the inner sanctum (garbhageha) is prescribed for the spiritual guides (deśikas),
while service to the half-pavilion (ardhamaṇṭapa) is declared for those learned in the Vedas (śrotriyas).
Beyond that [are the duties] of the Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, and beyond those is the service of the Śūdras.
Furthermore, the tailor, the one who controls speech, the one who crushes sesame seeds, and the butcher;
The carpenter, the goldsmith, the stonemason,
the blacksmith, the potter, and the cowherd— these indeed are the lower castes.
With these [deities], one must perform the act of seeing at the base of the banner;
however, the sight of low-caste individuals such as washermen must take place outside the temple.
In the case of a fine of one hundred [paṇas] for entering the fields of Caṇḍālas, Śvapacas, and others,

Furthermore, the absence of the presence of the gods gives rise to great calamity,
and a great pestilence enters [the city], affecting all the inhabitants of the town.

I shall describe the castes in their proper order; listen, O Brahmin, in brief.
One born from a Brāhmaṇa father and a Brāhmaṇī mother, having been consecrated by the sacraments, becomes a Brāhmaṇa.
In this same way, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras are to be known as born from their own respective wombs.
Likewise, [the duties of the first three are] teaching, studying, performing sacrifices, and officiating at sacrifices.
Giving and receiving [gifts]—these are the six duties of the first-born (the Brāhmaṇa).
Of these six duties, three are his means of livelihood.
Sacrificing for others, teaching, and receiving gifts from the pure;
as well as sacrificing, studying, and giving—these are the duties of the Vaiśya and the Kṣatriya.
(146) Receiving gifts is the primary duty of a Brāhmaṇa, as are officiating at sacrifices and teaching; likewise,
one born from a Brāhmaṇa father and a Kṣatriya mother is a Savarṇa Brāhmaṇa.
One should always study Āyurveda, Atharvaveda, and Dhanurveda;
[Āyurveda] for a Brāhmaṇa among the three [higher] castes, and [the other two] for a Kṣatriya among the two [lower] castes.
These six are recorded as the offspring of a Vaiśya from a single caste;
indeed, one born from a Brāhmaṇa according to the rule upon a Vaiśya woman is called an Ambaṣṭha.
He may live by agriculture, or likewise by the profession of a fire-priest;
or his livelihood may be that of a standard-bearer, for the Ambaṣṭhas are those who live by weapons.
From a Brahmin father and a Vaiśya mother is born one called a Kumbhakāra;
he may live by the profession of a potter or by that of a barber.
Shaving above the navel is therefore called *nāpita*;
one born from a Brāhmaṇa through a Śūdra woman according to the prescribed rule is considered a *pāraśava*.
It is taught that those who take refuge in Bhadrakālī shall live as her worshippers;
however, one born from theft in relation to her is proclaimed to be a Niṣāda.
Having killed wild beasts in the forest and making a living by selling their meat,
he was then born as a son from a Vaiśya woman who was a legal wife, according to the prescribed rite, by means of a king.
A Kṣatriya may live by the occupation of a Vaiśya, but he must not practice the [lower] mantras;
if he acts with theft in that very occupation, he is born as a jeweler.
One should perform the polishing of gems and the boring of pearls;
he who is born from the union of a Śūdra woman and a Kṣatriya is known as an Ugra according to tradition.
If the king, who wields the rod of punishment, should inflict punishment upon those who do not deserve it, he incurs sin.
However, the rule prescribed for a Vaiśya father and a Śūdra mother of a different caste is as follows: the son shall be a Karaṇa.
From a Māhiṣya father and a Karaṇī mother, a Rathakāra is born;
he performs various artisanal crafts as well as the construction of palaces.
The livelihoods of a chariot-maker consist of reading various treatises, working with gold and ornaments,
and likewise performing work in iron.
From a king, upon a Brāhmaṇa maiden, is born one named Sūta;
he is unworthy of the Vedas, yet he is an expounder of their duties.
From a Vaiśya with a Śūdra woman, a son named Deha is born;
from a Kṣatriya with a Vaiśya woman, a Māgadha is born, and from a Śūdra woman, a Kṣattṛ.
From a Śūdra, a Vaiśya woman gave birth to an Āyogava and a Vaitasa;
and from a Vaiśya through illicit union with a Nṛpa woman, one named a Pulinda is born.
By the killing of wicked beings, he should subsist in the forest;
from a Śūdra [woman] are born the Āyogava, the Kṣattṛ, and the Caṇḍāla, the lowest of men.
Just as a low-caste being is born from a Śūdra father and a Brāhmaṇī mother,
even more outside the pale than that outsider is one born from a member of the four castes.
Those born in the reverse order of castes are excluded from all ritual duties;
however, one born to an Ugra father from a Kṣatriya mother is known as a Śvapāka.
The dwelling of Caṇḍālas and dog-cookers is outside the village;
likewise, one should avoid a man who is covered by rain [and thus unrecognizable], or one of impure origin whose caste is unknown.
One may manifest as if noble through one's own actions, though actually ignoble;
for one born according to the sequence of the castes is indeed said to be "born in the natural order" (*anulomaja*).
That which is produced in the reverse order is called "pratiloma" (inverse).
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Discernment of the Description of the Conduct of the Sacred Fields," in the *Brahmayāmala*, the compendium of one hundred thousand verses.
Hereafter, I shall explain the supreme installation of the Child (Bāla),
whether in a temple that is broken or dilapidated, or likewise in the case of an image.
Thereafter, one should have it newly constructed, beautiful with paintings on all its parts;
then, at the time of entry, one should perform the ritual as previously prescribed.
One should perform the purification of the sacrificial pit, the pavilion, the temple, and the image;
O Goddess of the gods, install the deity according to the procedure prescribed in the Tantras.
Otherwise, I shall fully describe the supreme pure seat (śuddhāsana),
[to be performed] at an auspicious moment, under a favorable lunar mansion, a conjunction, and an astrological division (karaṇa).

At night, the wise practitioner should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) for the Goddess, the Mother, together with their respective sequences; the knower of the ritual should place the Queen of the Gods before the heap of grain.
One should prepare a yogapīṭha that is either circular or square;
there, one should worship with five droṇas of śāli rice in due order.
Upon that, the practitioner of mantra should place [the vessel] made of five *droṇas* of rice;
having made it square and even, he should sprinkle it with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
In the center of that, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp;
[and place] a jar made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay.
One should take nine water-pots that are well-baked and very firm,
and arrange them in sequence from Indra to Īśāna.
Having placed the water for sipping (ācamana) in the northeast with the mantra "Indra," and likewise in the center;
having placed the water for washing the feet (pādya) in the south, and the decoction (kaṣāya) in the southwest;
Having placed milk in the western direction, one should place curd in the northwestern direction;
having placed clarified butter in the northern direction, one should likewise place products of the cow in the northeastern direction.
One should place the goddesses beginning with Brāhmī there and cause them to be offered with their respective mantras:
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, and likewise Vaiṣṇavī.
Vārāhī, Māhendrī, and Īśvarī—
[the wise] know [these goddesses] in the ninth [position], as well as Ekavīrī in the middle of the jars.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite with perfumes, flowers, and incense,
one should place [the deity] well-composed in the center of the lotus, within the pericarp.
The knower of mantras should deposit the five jewels, beginning from the east, in the center of the *mātṛsthala* according to their respective conjunctions, using the nine seed-syllables.
Thereafter, one should fill it with water purified by a cloth and scented with fragrant substances;
having placed a tuft of grass and unbroken grains within, one should wrap it with a pair of cloths.
Having completely covered [the vessel] with blood, one should display the mantra and mudrā;
having thus consecrated the vases, one should thereafter become intent upon meditation.
Having meditated upon the earth as produced by cooking and the pericarp fashioned from Mount Meru,
one should place the Goddess of the Gods, the Mother of Beings, upon that pericarp.
She holds a skull and a khaṭvāṅga staff, sits upon a great corpse,
possesses four, eight, or three eyes, and has the form of Rudra.
The goddess, whose garment is the directions, with disheveled hair, adorned with great serpents,
wearing a garland of skulls, and possessing a radiance like the fire of universal destruction.
The wise man should install the Goddess, who bears such a form and strikes terror into both gods and demons, resembling ten million suns as her weapon, within the ritual jar.
There, the cessation [of the rite] should be performed, accompanied by mantra and mudrā;
one should offer the food-oblation according to the rule and commence the *yātrā-homa*.
One who has been initiated should perform the fire-oblation with either eight or five [kinds of fuel]:
the *bilva*, *palāśa*, *khadira*, *vaṭa*, and likewise the *audumbara*.
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with mantras according to the prescribed rule for the Plakṣa, Vikaṅkata, Aśvattha, and Vāruṇa trees in the directions starting from the east.
The wise man [should prepare] various kinds of sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) according to their characteristics;
that which is square belongs to Indra, while the one arising from the womb (yoni) is in the southeast.
In the southern direction, there is a half-moon; in the south-west, a triangle;
in the western direction, it should be known as a circle; and in the north-west, a hexagon.
In the north there is a lotus-shaped [pit], and in the northeast an eight-cornered one;
among these, the wise man should understand that the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is indeed prescribed.
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with each respective mantra and with those who bear the [deity's] form;
having offered one hundred and eight oblations, one should offer them with a similar [mantra] while suspended.
The preceptor should begin the fire-oblation for the deities at the head-region [of the image],
using sesame seeds, white mustard, priyaṅgu, rice, and parched grain.
Having offered clarified butter, one should offer [oblations] for all the [deities], including Bāla;
having offered one hundred and eight oblations for each of all the forms (mūrtis).
Having offered twice as much for the preceptor at the Puṇṭarunālaya temple,
the mantra-practitioner should install the mobile [liṅga] in the previously mentioned location,
having adorned the site of the Guru and the child with canopies and other ornaments.
Then, having obtained the appropriate place and time, the preceptor should establish it in the location for the *bāla* (the child).
Once established, the work should proceed; however, the location for the *bāla* must be determined by the preceptor.
Then the preceptor, together with the practitioners,
should slowly lift the jar while maintaining the recollection as before.
Having heated it at the entrance, one should slowly circumambulate;
having entered, the wise man should worship the goddesses in the places designated for children.
One should worship all the jars and install the trident;
having worshipped according to the rule, one should offer the food offering (naivedya) in accordance with the ritual injunctions.
One should cause all five types of offerings to be presented with the mantra;
thereafter, one should offer the great bali accompanied by the Bhūtakrūra mantra.
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Installation of the Child," in the *Brahmayāmala*, the compendium of one hundred thousand verses. 38.
Henceforth, I shall explain the procedural sequence for fasting (laṅghana),
specifically regarding women and Brahmins when fasting occurs through negligence.
The offering to the Solitary Heroine (Ekavīrī) should be performed with the shedding of blood;
for a Kṣatriya, however, one should cause the cutting of flesh with swords.
Alternatively, a wise man should offer one goat with abundant flesh;
likewise, upon transgressing against a Vaiśya, he should cause meat of equal measure to be given.
For crossing over [the boundary] of Śūdras, one should cause a fast of one month to be observed;
likewise for [riding] swans, cranes, buffaloes, dogs, donkeys, and camels.
Likewise, one should cause a horse, a rose-apple tree, a monkey and so forth, an elephant, a cock, and a firefly to be given.
If one transgresses against cattle, ascetics, or Brahmins,
one should offer one hundred and eight oblations and then cause a single goat to be sacrificed.
Or one should cause a Caṇḍāla to step over [the boundary] by means of transgressions such as walking against the grain;
then, an immediate execution must be carried out, with the sacred thread placed over the right shoulder.
One should offer oblations with the root gāyatrī mantra; this they know as the *yauvika* rite.
Having bypassed [the rites for] virgins, one hundred and eight oblations are offered.
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Rule for Wandering and Leaping through the City," in the *Brahmayāmala*, the compendium of one hundred thousand verses. 39.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the supreme characteristics of the image;
a wise man should have the image fashioned according to the measurement of nine *tālas*.
One should have it made of stone, metal, or even clay;
one should know that it has eight arms in a village and four arms in a city.
One should know the two-armed form in the midst of the forest, the sixteen-armed on the mountain peak,
one should fashion the twelve-armed in the ocean, and the six-armed in Jandandya.

She should be depicted as dark-complexioned and auspicious, with fangs like the teeth of Death, holding a trident, a skull-cup, a khaṭvāṅga staff, and likewise a ḍamaru drum— these eight [attributes].
