(154) Hereafter I shall proclaim the sequence of the ritual for the Kṣetrapāla,
the Lord of the three worlds, the omniscient one, the god of all gods, who has conquered his senses.
The form of Āgameśa is the protector of the primordial field (Ādikṣetra);
that supreme space is indeed the deity, and the mind itself.
One should constantly contemplate with the mind [the form] that is honored in the world of Śiva;
from that time forward, O Lord of Gods, it becomes auspicious, just like the form of Śiva himself.
Thereafter, one should know the Daṇḍālaya, which is the dissolution (pralaya) and the measure of the row;
it is the form of all living beings and the narrative concerning the end of the lineage of the eldest.
Within the *vṛtta* there should be light (*jyotis*), and within that light, an atom (*aṇu*);
likewise, within the atom is the *bindu*, which is the *kṣetrapāla* whose nature is Śiva.
Partless, stainless, peaceful, and characterized by the absence of conceptual proliferation;
partless yet possessing all parts, she is the deity of fragrance.
The Blessed One, the Supreme Lord, has arisen from all living beings.
Thus, there are three distinct forms: Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara;
yet in the world, Kṣetrapāla is seen for the sake of protecting merit.
The first should be the embodiment of knowledge; the second, the embodiment of peace;
the third should be the embodiment of wrath, possessing the qualities and defects of all beings.
Manifesting for the sake of protecting all beings in the world of mortals, one should install it there—
in the forest, in the cave, in the ocean, and on the mountain peak.
Whether at the confluence of rivers, in a forest retreat, or in a sheltered dwelling; whether in a village, a city, a town, or a market settlement.
Likewise, one should cause a *kolaka* to be placed upon the *droṇa* as a sign of fortune;
that specific scripture prescribes the location within the field according to the appropriate application.
I shall explain the remaining ritual actions in their proper sequence:
those for pacification, for nourishment, for portents, and for investigation.
One should perform the rite for pacification (śāntika) in a village or other inhabited places;
one should perform the rite for nourishment (pauṣṭika) in a cave or a forest dwelling.
The wondrous supreme form and the protection against malevolent magic should be performed with the appropriate yoga in each respective place as is fitting.
The four-armed form is for pacification (śāntika), while the eight-armed form is for nourishment (pauṣṭika);
the two-armed form is common to all rites; the remaining ritual procedure is prescribed accordingly.
He is four-armed; in his right hands there is a trident and a ḍamaru drum, while in his left hand a skull-cup is prescribed as an armlet.
O Lord, it is ordained that he stands upon a lotus-seat surrounded by his attendants;
his feet are said to rest upon a mountain, and his waist is encircled by serpents.
On the sides, there is a binding of cords made of gold and jewels;
on the belly, there is a serpent-binding accompanied by a central knob.
With a human head hanging from his mouth down to his ear, wearing the sacred thread over all his limbs,
and with three long strands between his breasts like the crescent moon.
That vajra is three-eyed and equal [to that], with a blazing radiance from its upward-pointing hair;
above the forehead is a human head, encircling it according to the prescribed sequence.
He is described as having an earring, or perhaps a single leaf-ornament;
his hair is encircled by serpents, and he has red eyes and red hair.
Having adorned the Bālacakra and likewise the white peak,
[he whose] face is like the full moon is endowed with splendor.
Eight-armed, with a noose in the right [hand].
Having fashioned the skull-bowl, the hand-drum, the Pināka bow, and the sword according to the previously mentioned procedure, one should likewise fashion the ornaments in the same manner.
The ritual for nourishment (pauṣṭika) should be known as relying on the ninth deity;
his form is that of a spirit (bhūta), with two arms, holding a staff in his right hand.
Having placed a skull on the left, adorned with ornaments made of spirits,
one should establish the abode of the Kṣetrapāla in that location by means of Īśa.
The form of Yoga is ten tālas; the gentle form is nine tālas;
the form of the Earth is four tālas; and one tāla is prescribed for the remaining [form].

The *śāntika* [mandala] has a lotus pedestal and its fierce corner should likewise be so; it should be established with four arms, which brings auspiciousness and fulfills all purposes. Sons and friends increase, and it is the means for accomplishing all desires and goals.
It should be known as four-armed, auspicious, and the bringer of peace to the village;
having performed the rite for nourishment (*pauṣṭika*), it indeed possesses the power to destroy enemies.
It should be known as the "increase of women" (strīvardhana) and is remembered as the "form of the elements" (bhūtākāra).
For the benefit of the world and the non-world, one should join the effect with the cause in every action.

Having performed the rite of the *balikarma*, the wise ones should apply all the necessary procedures, such as the ritual bathing and so forth, as prescribed for the rite of pacification (*śāntikarma*).
Having performed the rite of consecration (adhivāsa), one should employ all the ritual substances;
having performed the installation of the vase (kalaśa), the wise one utters the syllable *phaṭ*.
Thus should be the consecration mantra, while recollecting the root mantra;
likewise, the "great image" (mahābera) is the root, and here the "syllable of life" (jīvākṣara) is spoken of.
One should place the root syllable Oṃ in the center; it is said that the syllable Śrīṃ is [placed] there.
One should place the ending Svāhā there, and at the front, the syllable Strīṃ is said [to be placed].
The wise one should place scents and flowers, and cause incense and lamps to be offered; thereafter, he should station the preceptor together with the deity.
At the periphery of the essence of Brahmā, from the root of the sun, are the moon and the sun;
likewise, having placed Viṣṇu in the center, there are the forms that effect the dissolution of all things.
One should install the Lord Sadāśiva, who possesses a great body, is the protector of the field, and is known as Brahmajñāna, conjoined with Indra.
He knows the Brahmāvāla, the Jitriyāja, and the Dvivṛddhi;
[he knows] the throat, the heart, the feet, the navel, the secret organ, the head, and the crown of the head.
Having repeatedly placed the syllable *oṃ*, one should arrange the mantra;
one should cause the Brahmins to pronounce the words of auspiciousness and cause all musical instruments to resound.
Again, one should duly worship the ninefold Kṣetrapāla according to the rules.
Having performed the rite prescribed in the scriptures, the installation is auspicious and brings about prosperity.
Just as an action perishes through the loss of its locus by means of its characteristic mark—
thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Kṣetrapāla," in the *Brahmayāmala-śatasahasra-saṃhitā*. 41.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the compendium of the Mothers’ tridents:
the northern, the southern, the downward-facing, and likewise the upward-facing.
One should avoid the southern solstice as well as the six-month period;
the northern [solstice] is declared to be ever superior, for it encompasses everything.
Thus, these constitute the compendium of the Śūla, which accomplishes all desires and aims;
it brings about abundance of food, security, health, and the increase of all crops.
Beneficial to the four castes and destroying all calamities,
it brings auspicious peace to everything, whether in a village or even in a city.
Gold, silver, iron, and likewise a wooden trident;
half of what is made of clay; and the acquisition of a house for a muhūrta.

(159) And there were words of benediction (*svastivācana*), as well as the chanting of the Vedas (*brahmaghoṣa*); likewise, there were drums (*paṭaha*), maddala drums, cymbals (*tāla*), and *karaṭītimilā* drums.
Likewise, one should provide a conch shell together with a black [pig], as well as the sound of the Mothers,
along with the preceptor and his disciples, and garments and ornaments.
The previously mentioned rite of depositing the sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) is for the purpose of consecration (adhivāsana);
that which is joined with the Mother’s Pavilion (mātṛmaṇḍapa) is for the rite of pacification (śāntikarman).
One should prepare a sacrificial mound there, using eight *droṇas* of *śāli* rice,
half that amount of husked rice, and likewise half that amount of sesame seeds.
Its half should be joined with sesame seeds and spread out with a handful of *darbha* grass;
in its center, one should draw a lotus adorned with all ornaments.
Having likewise made an area equal to four squares, measuring one cubit in dimension, [one should plant] the Aśvattha, Udumbara, Plakṣa, and Vaṭa trees.
On the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila), the preceptor, together with the practitioners, should place the seat;
he should then offer water for the feet, water for sipping, and perform worship with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
Having worshipped with all the mantras according to the prescribed ritual, beginning with water for the feet, one should offer as the sacrificial oblation goat’s blood, meat, and so forth.

The practitioner, the preceptor, and the disciple should offer the remains of the flowers (*nirmālya*) and all other offerings, and then dismiss them with the *sadyojāta* mantra. They should also offer betel leaf (*tāmbūla*) using the same mantra.
O Teacher, this is the practice for the seat of death belonging to the mantra;
it consists of circumambulating the temple and performing circumambulation.
And likewise, having circumambulated the preceptor, who possesses all the Mothers,
[he should worship] Sadāśiva and Śiva.
The Vasus with eight, the Ādityas with twelve,
and all eleven Rudras are likewise endowed with the Aśvinī constellation.
May Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Soma, Īśa, and likewise Anya come; salutations, salutations!
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī,
as well as Vārāhī, Indrāṇī, Cāmuṇḍī, Gaṇa, and Rudrakā.
Thus, these are the *māṇas* in sequence; salutations again and again!
Then there are Yoginī, Ḍākinī, Sākinī, and Pūtanā.
Pālinī, Dundubhī, and likewise Ucchiṣṭā are the Mothers;
as well as the Bhūtas, Pretas, Piśācas, and Vetālas.
The Kumāragrahakūṣmāṇḍa, Mahādeva, and likewise the Grahas;
all of them, the entire world, and all the deities of every sacred seat (pīṭha).
May the thirty-two lords also come; homage, homage!
[I salute] the preceptor joined with the mantra, as well as the disciples and the Saṃhitā.
Having performed the ritual placement (vinyāsa) of Mahākāla and the assembly of the circle of Mothers,
one should perform the second [placement], endowed with the proper characteristics, which consists of the collection of the artisan's arrows.
The journey of the pedestal and bowl, or the two [parts] made by the artisan upon the pedestal,
should be endowed with all auspicious characteristics and possessed of the marks of skilled craftsmen.
p.
161) These, in their respective order, constitute the trident and the house of the planets;
they possess all the characteristics according to the rules of the artisan and the painter.
The characteristics for Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras are as follows:
the Śūdra measure is ten tālas, while for a Brāhmaṇa it is nine tālas; however, for a Kṣatriya, it is nine tālas.
The Vaiśya [should be] eight tālas, and the Śūdra seven tālas;
the sword is on the left and right, and the trident-leaf is in the middle.
The leaf-sword and the face should each have a width of four finger-breadths;
they should be two tālas in height, of all colors, and likewise fixed upon a trident.
The tip [of the spout] should have a mouth ten finger-breadths wide, and the mouth of the pedestal eight finger-breadths;
the pedestal itself should be sixteen finger-breadths in height, square in shape, and constitute the support for the pedestal.
Endowed with all auspicious marks and variegated petals,
this is the supreme rite for pacification and the installation of Kālī.
Endowed with all the primary marks, it is variegated and manifold in every way.
One should place the entire body, joined with all its parts, characterized by the arts and painting,
as well as the trident-leaf and the Brahma-Brahman of the god.
The left petal is likewise in the northeast, and the right is the Viṣṇu-petala;
these are the presiding deities, or rather, the deities of the trident-petaled [mandala].
Śūlapīṭha and Mahākāla are prescribed for the center;
one should also install Bahuvīra at the seat of the weapon (astrapīṭha).
The staff of the principal seat is indeed the footstool presided over by that [deity].
For the purpose of pacification, its width should be one-third or even one part.
The handle joined to the mouth is sixteen finger-breadths in width;
the bell is one-third of that in width, and it is endowed with all the auspicious characteristics.
The width of the footstool should be two tālas and four aṅgulas;
it should be decorated with all manner of paintings and drawings, featuring eight petals and a pericarp.
Joined with the left side, [it is] Manonmanī, ending with me;
it has thirty-two deities as its presiding divinities, the innermost of the inner deities.
In the middle of the staff of the gods is the eighth, Adhiyoginī;
thus these, in due order, constitute the collection of the trident.
Whether a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra, [this rite] bestows the increase of sons;
it is meritorious, beneficial to all the world, and supremely conducive to universal peace.
It destroys all diseases and eliminates all portents of death;
it [gives mastery over] a village and the lord of the village, as well as the *śūla* and *saṃgraha* [fevers].
It is for the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas; it is the performer, the sustainer, and the cause of prosperity.
It is the pacifier of the great pestilence and the destroyer of diseases caused by wind.
There shall be abundance of food, growth of villages, and the flourishing of all crops;
even that which is deficient in mantra, deficient in ritual action, or likewise deficient in materials [shall become complete].
A time deficient by even a muhūrta, as well as a fraction of a moment (kālakala), possesses every defect; therefore, it must specifically be avoided in all circumstances.
The worship of the iron [linga] and the trident for the sake of iron, consisting of a mere trident—
thus ends the procedure for the installation of the trident in the *Brahmayāmala*, in the compendium of one hundred thousand verses, titled "The Procedure for the Installation of the Trident."
The forty-second chapter. || 42 ||

Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the sequence of rules for expiation (prāyaścitta) regarding the pacification of the Mothers (mātṛśānti) in their conjunctions, according to the occurrence of specific faults.
For the sake of pacifying those defects,
there is a determination of atonement regarding a temple that is broken, shattered, or has fallen down over time.
Whether it be a stone image, or even one that is wounded or broken,
or pierced by others, or fallen, or indeed shattered.
One who is low-born, or even diseased, [should not perform the rites for] a dwelling, an image, or likewise a gateway; nor [should one do so] when two suns appear together with their radiance.
Whether it be the shaking of the earth or its burning by fire,
the practitioner who has taken the pledge, along with his spiritual sons and the venerable master, [should perform it].
Where there is a seat for the patron afflicted by disease, or thorny *citraka* trees on all sides,
or where it is deficient in sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), or even lacking in the *hanu* (jaw/structure), [that site is unsuitable].
But if it is devoid of gold or devoid of cloth, that [image] should not be recognized as the form of the deity; [in such a case], an excellent expiation (prāyaścitta) is prescribed.
With the nine-syllable mantra, one hundred and eight oblations of each substance—from sacrificial fuel sticks down to sesame seeds—are offered; thus the Gāyatrī of the Goddess is sacrificed.
When the palace or the pavilion is damaged, one should perform eight hundred oblations, accompanied by the nine Śaktis, using the trident and the other eight weapons.
One should designate a ruined or inferior temple as a site for novices;
there, the preceptor, together with artisans, should construct a temple.
Then one should perform the sprinkling according to the previously mentioned procedure;
and in that case, where the oblation was deficient, one should cause the root mantra to be recited.
And at the conclusion of the installation of the Mothers, [the rite is performed] in a place beautified with plaster, paintings, and the like;
[it is forbidden] in the presence of outcastes, those of low caste, or in a state of defilement caused by the touch of a dog.
Even those of mixed castes other than the [four] primary ones, as well as the outcaste and the insane;
and even a door-panel that is broken, cracked, or split, or the two pillars themselves.
The ritual sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa) should be performed as prescribed by the rules, as before,
at the outskirts of villages and cities when men are afflicted by disease.
Therefore, perform the sprinkling with effort directed toward all faces;
however, one should not do it in that manner, but according to the previously stated procedure.
The wise man should perform the *pumsavana* rite according to the previously mentioned procedure;
he should likewise perform the ceremonial bath (*snapana*) at that very same time, in accordance with his means.
In that very place, the wise mantra-practitioner, having abandoned that [previous rite], should perform nine thousand and one hundred and eight oblations with the nine-syllable mantra.
In that very context, one should perform the threefold fire offering (homa)—the superior and so forth—in due order;
all substances are for pacifying rites, especially the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
p.

165) O Teacher, for one who has contracted a disease, or is afflicted by illness, one should perform a fire-oblation with sesame seeds mixed together using the root mantra; [the disease] should be abandoned [through this rite].
When burning with fire a garment, a dwelling, or even an image,
one should perform a fire-oblation (homa) for all such objects combined with the nine-syllable mantra.
In the event of an earthquake, or during diseases and quarrels,
as well as when a gateway collapses, one should perform [the rite] joined with the root mantra.
One should perform the oblation with twenty-five offerings, each offered separately,
using the nine-syllable mantra as well as the *uttālaka* mantra.
In the event of contact with a Caṇḍāla, one should avoid a vessel that has been broken;
however, having set aside another vessel, one should join it with the syllable Om (praṇava).
The ritual procedure for sprinkling with water [is performed] by means of beds or deaths;
or [it is performed] by dogs, or by those of Mleccha birth, or by artisans in the work of painting.
If one enters within the precincts of the Ālaya, it becomes a cause for fault;
therefore, an expiation must be performed, and one should carry out a ritual sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa).
At the time of worshipping the goddesses, he proceeds according to the specific fault [of the victim],
whether it be a linga, an image, an axe, or even a trident.
A bell, a water-pot, a bow, and an arrow,
as well as other weapons, are likewise placed among the offerings for the children.
If [the vessel] has fallen or been broken through negligence, it is considered [to be restored] according to what is possible;
having taken [materials] as they are available and having offered them, one should present them to the Goddess.
Having offered oblations with the root mantra, one should again begin the circumambulation.
The celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial omens portend the destruction of the enemy.
If there are crows or even cocks, or if the chains [are broken], or if there is fear of a great wind, or where the human [life] is long... [the omen is unfavorable].
Or there may be conflict with human beings... [omission].

Where there is deficiency due to negligence, however, one should perform the rite fully equipped with all the prescribed measures, reciting the root Gāyatrī mantra one thousand times or one hundred and eight times.
Whether it be one's own army or an enemy army, so that agitation or battle may occur,
one should perform the fire oblation with the mantra of the Goddess Gāyatrī and the root-vidyā.
Whether using a sacrificial ladle, or even a vessel for oblation materials, or a golden image,
one should offer the *kālittha* or the *laḍa* with the root mantra.
If, having established the pitcher, it should fall through negligence,
the wise man should perform a fire-oblation (homa) with that very same nine-syllable mantra.
Through the consecration of the bathing rite, even a broken jar [is purified];
for when a defect arises therein, it occurs within that single central jar.
If the banner falls or if the staff of the banner is broken,
one should perform a fire-offering (homa) there with the Vidyā-mantra beginning with "samayādyā."
Where, upon the cutting of animals, the image of a calf is seen within the belly,
there is a specific expiation for the purpose of pacifying that fault.
Having performed the recitation and the ritual sprinkling, the wise one should then commence the festival;
he should perform the festival for seven days, every single day.
The ceremonial bathing (snapana) should be performed according to the injunctions of the scriptures;
one should perform the respective rites of pacification (śānti), as well as those for the increase of progeny and the destruction of enemies.
One who is afflicted by disease should first perform the fire-oblation according to the rules for that which causes all suffering and is eternal, and then apply it to the primary forms.
However, in the case of one who is devoid of constant festivals and likewise devoid of the *sandhi* (conjunctions),
one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) joined with the root mantra and other elements.
In the case of one who has neglected worship, [the penance] may be one, fifteen, or eighteen [days];
by means of a month, one should perform nine, fifty, or eight hundred [repetitions].
If [a snake] bites once every half-month, one should bathe according to the prescribed rite;
but at the end of a month, a year, or so forth, the expiation (prāyaścitta) must be performed according to the rule.
If one does not worship once, twice, or thrice a day,
or if one fails to worship the Goddess and the others for eleven nights, [the rite] is severed.
If [the rite] is performed at a time devoid of the proper hour, one should undertake its pacification;
if it should exceed the proper hour, there will be an increase in the oblations (*homāda*).
When, upon being questioned in reverse and direct order regarding a person's deficient knowledge and insight,
it is found that men in either a village or a city are afflicted by disease;
Therefore, O Goddess, with every effort one should perform an expiation that brings about her presence,
and likewise one that is free from musical instruments.
If the *kara-mudrā* is omitted, or if the site for the *homa* becomes unsuitable, or if,
during the time of the dance, a person should fall due to negligence;
Likewise, having slain the sacrificial animal according to the prescribed rite, one should perform the fire-oblation;
or else, offer a thousand oblations of clarified butter and likewise perform the pacification of the field (kṣetraśānti).

Therefore, beginning with the dance, one should perform the circumambulation of the villages and other sites, as well as the cleansing and striking; however, one should avoid [striking] the goddesses.
If the cleansing is deficient, there will be flogging and the loss of one's position;
therefore, with every effort, one should perform the propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma).
Then, one should not step over the remaining musical instruments, such as the *paṭaha* and others, nor over living beings ranging from humans down to flies, in their respective order.
But if one has transgressed through negligence, one should offer oblations and present them to the Goddess;
then, having meditated upon Śiva as the nine fires, one should worship him and perform the placement of the root-mantra.
But having bypassed others, one should worship the Goddess there;
for the festival that is celebrated in this direction maintains the threefold human prowess.
"Great faults arise; I declare that [the woman] is impure.
I shall describe the atonement according to the nature of the fault; the wise man should perform the pacification."
One who is well-composed should perform all the rites for the consecration at the proper time;
having thus examined [the site] in many ways, the most excellent of men should cause it to be constructed there.
One should properly honor the teacher with garments, gold, and finger-rings.
Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Rule for Expiation," in the *Brahmayāmala-śatasahasra-saṃhitā*. 43.
(170) O Brahmin, listen as I describe the characteristics of the trident (śūla) in due order,
as well as the dimensions of the image in its superior, middling, and inferior forms.
That which ends at the navel and extends upward to the forehead is the best;
that which is half of that should be known as the middle, and half of that again is the medium [smaller] size.
Therefore, one should draw the middle line like a half-moon;
the middle section should be fashioned so that it forms a middle portion.
On the creeper of the middle portion, there should indeed be the three-eyed one;
the neck is the syllable of the pedestal, and Brahmāṇī is on the four-armed [form] with eyes.
Endowed with four faces, with an eye in each face,
accompanied by a garland of lotuses, and adorned with a black antelope skin.
One should meditate upon the Goddess, wearing the sacred thread (*upavīta*),
seated either upon a lotus throne or a swan throne.
Holding a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) in the left hand and a rosary (akṣasūtra) in the right,
possessing such a form and endowed with these characteristics;
and above the eyes, the two eyes indeed possessed of the Vaiṣṇava marks.
Joined with a black serpent as a garland, likewise endowed with eight arms,
adorned with necklaces and armlets, and decorated with red garments.
One should install such a three-eyed image of peaceful form;
it should be fashioned according to the prescribed rite and endowed with the proper characteristics in the north-western direction.
By means of the two portions on the sides, side-pain (pārśva-śūla) occurs as it should;
and by means of the side of the middle portion, side-pain occurs as it should.
In that [mandala], the trident and the *bāhula* are described in sequence according to their respective proportions;
one should cause the width of their base to be made with eight parts.
The thickness of those [fingers] is said to be one-eighth or one-sixteenth [of their length];
however, in certain parts, it may be half of that, following the gradual sequence.
The wise man, endowed with the defining characteristics, should rotate [the instrument] extended;
he should cause it to revolve at that point on the side of the middle section.
Likewise, the wise one [should place] two parts in the middle as the two mouth-cavities;
from the base, it should have three parts according to the divisions of the trident.
The neck-base (grīvā-pīṭha) should be made square and very beautiful;
its thickness should be one-seventh of the width of the base.
It is adorned with the birthplaces of sages such as Kauśika at the corners of the pedestals,
provided with a network of bells, and beautified by leaves of the *pippalī* tree.
The neck shall likewise be the pedestal, endowed with secondary ornaments;
indeed, one should eliminate the pedestal from both sides by means of two parts.
Just as there may be slight cutting or other defects at the edge of a side-ornament (pārśvaśūla), that trident (śūla) must indeed be fashioned out of gold alone; it shall truly become a deity.
Both gold and silver [are used];
however, gold is said to be for the stake (śūla), while it should be made with silver for the royal stake (rājadaṃśūla).
The middle [triśūla] should be known as being made of silver; that is proclaimed to be the middling one. A wise person should have the entire trident fashioned out of silver.
The lowest trident (śūla) is said to be fashioned from pure [metal] alone;
it should be entirely auspicious in form and endowed with [the proper] proportions.
Relying upon one of these [sites], the most wealthy person should have it constructed there;
it should be free from pits and the like, and devoid of insects and hollows.
There, the wise and learned one should arrange it according to its detailed form;
it should be made with a seat, beautiful in its core and middle.
One part of that is proclaimed as the triple-stemmed stalk and the weapon;
one-third of the neck-section is proclaimed as its circumference.
The pedestal of Vīrabhadra should indeed be established according to the prescribed ritual;
its width is proclaimed to be half of that [of the previous].
The width is proclaimed to be one part of all the sections, and the thickness is likewise proclaimed;
the height of the pedestal itself is proclaimed to be one part of the circumference.
The neck of the pedestal should have a shape similar to that at the bottom;
it should be square above and have its corners extended at the base.
It should be circular in shape, held above and below;
thus the pedestal (pīṭha) should be fashioned, adorned with lotuses at the top and bottom.
One should install Vīrabhadra and the other Mothers upon the trident-seat;
thus indeed has the characteristic of the trident been declared in brief.
p.
173) One should perform the rite beginning with the placement of the embryo (*garbha*) according to the ritual actions prescribed in the scriptures;
in this very manner, it should be performed, endowed with the characteristics of the trident (*śūla*).
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Characteristics of the Trident," in the *Brahmayāmala*, the compendium of one hundred thousand verses. 44.
I shall now proclaim the installation of the trident; listen, O Brahmin, according to the proper sequence.
One should perform it in front of the temple, and especially in the northeast.
One should have a pavilion constructed there, measuring nine cubits, seven cubits, or even five cubits, according to the rites prescribed in the scriptures.
The wise man should construct a square pavilion endowed with the proper characteristics, having recourse to one of three types.
One should have a pavilion constructed there, measuring nine cubits, seven cubits, or even five cubits;
two types of pavilions are prescribed, and in the northern one, there should be a seat.
It is provided with sixteen pillars and endowed with four archways.
The width of the goddess is said to be five parts or three parts;
its height is one part of that, resembling the surface of a mirror.
It should be provided with three girdles and endowed with all auspicious characteristics;
when one should make it with a single girdle, [then...]
The first has been declared to me, and it is called the "Proclaimed First" (Ādyaprakīrtitā).
Therefore, it is proclaimed that [the finger] less than one digit, or even two [less],
is declared to be the middle [finger].
The height has thus been stated; now the width is being described.
It is proclaimed as being beautiful and provided with staircases on all sides.
The height has thus been stated; therefore, the width is now being described.
O Brahman, there should be a staircase in each of the four directions, following the sequence of the cardinal points.
It was provided with four gates, draped with garlands of *darbha* grass,
covered over the threshing floor, and adorned with flower garlands.
Equipped with incense and lamps, and provided with archways,
[one should plant] the Plakṣa, Udumbara, Aśvattha, and Vaṭa trees in order from the east onwards.
The *plakṣa* tree should be for the eastern archway, and that of *udumbara* wood for the southern;
the *aśvattha* is to be known for the western, and the *vaṭa* is proclaimed for the northern.
Thus indeed should the archway (toraṇa) be known, endowed with its characteristic marks;
it is fixed upon the ground and extends four cubits upward.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite a water-pot (kalaśa) provided with an archway and endowed with the proper characteristics, at the base of those [trees].
Having thus constructed the pavilion, perform the installation of the banner;
the Guru should raise the banner beforehand, even without the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana).
Having raised the banner according to the ritual procedure, one should prepare a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) there;
the wise practitioner should likewise fashion the sacrificial mound within the *devikā*.
One should arrange a lotus in the midst of the very same one-increasing steps;
within that, one should decrease by one step at every single interval.
One should scatter rice grains mixed with *droṇa* seeds all around,
adorned with lotuses and with sesame seeds in the center.
One should fashion that lotus, complete with a pericarp and endowed with all characteristics,
as a seat there according to the ritual procedure seen in the scriptures.
Endowed with the five teachers, or otherwise accompanied by them,
and interspersed with the eight auspicious signs, perform the auspicious rite.
The trident should indeed be provided with a water-channel and endowed with the proper characteristics.

Having thus performed the ritual procedure, the wise one should install the trident (śūla) all around the altar (vedikā), starting from the direction of Indra (the east) and proceeding in order: the eastern [section] should be square,
while that in the southeast (pāvaka) should be in the shape of a womb (yoni).
The southern [direction] should be a half-moon; the south-western (nairṛta) should be a triangle;
the western (vāruṇa) is to be known as circular; and the north-western (vāyugocara) is a hexagon.
In the north, [the area] should be lotus-like in form, and in the northeast, an eight-cornered [figure];
within these, the fire-oblation (homa) should be performed according to the ritual prescribed in the scriptures.
One should offer sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, curd, milk, honey, and parched grain in successive order.
Then, at the clear dawn, one should begin the installation of the ritual stake (śūla).
The preceptor, whose very form is the mantra, should establish [the image] with the Mātṛ-mantra.
O fair-faced one, the wise [practitioner] should [place it] upon the altar in the center of that pavilion—
an altar that is beautiful and described in the scriptures.
At the time following the installation of the jewels, one should establish the *śūla* there;
at its conclusion, one should perform the ceremonial bath (*snapana*), and at the end, one should cast the offering to the spirits (*bhūtabali*).
In the afternoon, at its conclusion, the sacrifice was performed according to the prescribed order.
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Installation of the Trident," in the *Brahmayāmala*, the compendium of one hundred thousand verses.
